utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1524, first of all, I wish to ascertain your profession. In the introduction to your statement which you gave on the 11th of November and 5th of December, you said you work as an isolation mechanic for isolation devices -- insulation. And then you say you went to a higher pedagogical school, is that right, at Dula?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The highest school for defectology in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say in Belgrade you attended a course for work with handicapped children, especially with minors who are delinquents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Afterwards, as you say in paragraph 4, you worked in the financial and personnel department. I don't want to give the name of the factory, but it was in Zvornik, not to disclose your identity, but that is by and large what you did professionally speaking; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that there's been some misunderstanding here in the translation because mention is made of the military academy here and I assume that you didn't mean the military academy but school for reserve officers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did that during your regular military service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I understood it that you were very active in the organisation for reserve officers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are the questions you dealt with, and defence matters; is that right? Now let's clear up one more point in this regard: You never worked in the JNA. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not actively, no, but as a reserve officer, until I became a member of the Territorial Defence, that was the operative unit within the composition of -- or, rather, one-third were active soldiers, active-duty soldiers, and the rest were reservists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a reserve officer you were involved and engaged like any other men. You didn't have any special activities or assignments, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In paragraph 7 you say that in 1991, a lieutenant colonel called you, approached you, and he said that he was in charge of morale and political matters and moral guidance in the garrison and asked you whether you wanted to be a volunteer in Croatia. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when was that exactly? Do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in the summer of 1991, but I can't give you an exact date, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that he called you individually so that the JNA would cover up its true reasons for its involvement in Croatia. Is that something that you were able to deduce in talking to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did manage to conclude some things from talking to him, but I think that the things he asked me, the kinds of things he asked me was what he asked other reserve officers too. They were asked the same kinds of questions, whether they would like to take part as volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But nothing was secret or clandestine in any way, because I assume that you know that the JNA never covered up its involvement in Croatia in any way. It was present there, it was active there as the legitimate armed force in conformity with the Yugoslav constitution; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. I didn't say it was covering up anything, but the talks that were conducted did have a certain level of confidentiality to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where do you get the idea that talks like that were confidential?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was never called up officially. I never was officially invited to attend the meeting. It went through the TO headquarters. And it is common knowledge how army officers and reserve officers are called up. There is an official written invitation unless it is a mobilisation, and then calls up for the mobilisation take place, and they're not done in the way this was done, not how they approached me to come in and have a talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as the majority, as you say, talked about these things, do you know that the mobilisation of the reserve officers corps was conducted in June, as early on as June 1991 and that this related to everyone, not especially to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the mobilisation? The mobilisation was never put into effect in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you remember the name of that lieutenant colonel from the barracks, from the Tuzla barracks who talked to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't really make an effort to learn his name. Perhaps I did know it at the time, but a lot of time has gone by since then and I wouldn't be able to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 7 you also say that you knew that the JNA did not contact the members of other ethnic groups. "I was aware no other nationalities were approached in the same way, and if they had, I'm sure I would have found out about it." That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I heard about was that they were all Serbs, and on the other hand, during that period of time the Muslims did not wish to respond at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the point, isn't it? What I'm asking you is do you know how many official invitations went out and were tried to -- people tried to send out to members of other ethnic groups, other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a larger number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, on the basis of political instructions, I assume you know, the majority of Muslims refused to respond to the military obligations they were invited to assume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, going on to paragraph 8, you say that at that time there was a growing tension between Muslims and Serbs in the Zvornik area, and you say that everybody knew that there would be a war, but nobody knew exactly when it would break out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that in fact mean, and I deduce this from what you say, that war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was unavoidable, and that was common knowledge both to the Muslims and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether it was unavoidable, that would be a debatable point, because whenever a war -- if a war hasn't broken out yet it can be stopped if there is goodwill on all sides, and there was no goodwill on either side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what you mean when you say there was no goodwill on either side? What -- how did the Serbs behave and how did the Muslims behave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the two sides were afraid of each other. And in the winter of 1992 when the Ramadan festivities were being -- were taking place, the Muslims would frequent their mosques, but individuals were already armed at that time, individuals of the Muslim population. They would stand guard around the mosques. Of course they were armed. They had pistols, automatic weapons, or whatever they had, and there was sporadic shooting around town frequently, in the centre of town especially from that ethnic group, and also around Zvornik as well. There was retaliation and fire on both sides from the places where Serbs lived. So fear was growing from one day to the next. People were becoming afraid, those of them who weren't armed. And I assume that the city population wasn't keen to have a war at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, from what you've been saying, in the town of Zvornik itself, what could be seen out on the streets was in fact armed Muslims, and they gathered mostly around the mosques; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any armed Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not around the mosques, no, but as -- I've already told you where they were. They were in the suburbs or settlements several hundred metres away, in those districts and the slopes around Zvornik, in fact, where these settlements were. So from time to time there would be bursts of gunfire from that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as the town itself is concerned, there were just the Muslim forces in town. That's right, isn't it? According to what you yourself were able to see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not Muslim forces, just Muslim individuals who were armed in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from what point in time, roughly speaking, would you say that you saw these armed Muslims standing round the mosques and generally speaking an atmosphere of that kind where it became clear to the inhabitants of the Zvornik municipality that something was about to happen, or happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was at the beginning of the month of Ramadan, when the fast began, and when they were quite open, standing guard in front of the mosques because they said they were afraid that some Serbs might throw a bomb into the mosques. That was the justification and explanation they gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was there any incidents that occurred prior to that which gave rise to the sentiments and this justification for what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no direct incidents, no, but there were some things like when a taxi driver went missing and small incidents that took place on a daily basis without necessarily being ethnically based or provoked on ethnic grounds, but not direct ones, no, just indirect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this arming and deployment of Muslims around certain points in town was not caused by any particular incident that the Serbs had caused vis-a-vis the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Now, whether they had been deployed or whether these people on their own initiative individually took up their positions where they happened to be, where these people were standing who were armed, as I say, they were individuals. There was no kind of unit at all, numerous unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I can see from your statement that you spent a large part of your time socialising both with the Muslims and the Serbs, and there was no - how shall I put this? - in this socialising and social contacts around town, there were no divisions along those lines. People socialised normally, lived together normally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Until the war actually broke out - even the night before the war - we were on watches together around buildings. People who weren't armed did their best to protect their thresholds, their families and children, so we would stay up all night, standing watch in front of the buildings, both sides, the Muslims and the Serbs, because we didn't know who would be attacking or why or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, what you did standing guard and standing watch in front of your buildings, as you say, there were Serbs and Muslims there or mostly Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody, all sorts, both. However, during that period of time, rather just two or three days prior to the war, just before the war broke out, most of the population, if they had anywhere to go to leave Zvornik, they did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that you at that time when all this tension started were with, they were mostly Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were both Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the preparations that were under way within this Muslim community or, rather, the Party of Democratic Action and the Patriotic League, any preparations that were going on linked to the conflicts, anything as a forerunner to what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I do know is by talking to people. I had a lot of friends on both sides, so I talked to them. I know that both sides were arming themselves and preparing themselves and that that started straight after the New Year. Anybody who could get weapons got them, whether legally or illegally or however the weapons were procured, but both sides were busy arming themselves as far as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the activities of the Party of Democratic Action and the Patriotic League, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was friends with a narrow circle of people who were in the SDA party, and there wasn't any national division, ethnic division. And by -- from talking to them during the conversations we had, we were sort of speculating what could happen. They said, "Well, we're armed and you're armed." That was common knowledge. So it wasn't any secret. Everybody was wondering what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Abdulah Music, vice-president of the SDA in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I knew him. We even visited each other at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was trying to talk you into joining the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that he was trying to talk me into it. It was sort of a friendly conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you join in on that side; more or less along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the SDS or the SDA did not have a right-wing orientation. Quite simply, they represented two political communities, and they were supposed to give people who could do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was my understanding that this Abdulah Music - how should I put this? - suggested to you that you should join the SDS because, as you say yourself, he considered you to be a respectable man, an honest man, and that would have contributed to better cooperation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he was too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I think about him, too. We were friends. We visited each other at home, and we even trusted each other with our children. So it was a mutual thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time precisely Abdulah Music, together with another friend and neighbour of yours, Dr. Asim Juzbasic, Tica, actively worked on the arming of the Muslim population of the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not at that time. You're asking me about a particular time when I joined in. But this was almost a year before that. But at the time when they were being armed, both sides were being armed in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically now when you say they were arming themselves at a particular point at time. Do you know that this Music together with this Juzbasic actively worked on the arming of the Muslim population of the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And do you know that it is precisely Asim Juzbasic and Izet Mehinagic, an activist of the SDP and director of the Paruga company, Tuzla, Zvornik, on the 10th of April, 1992 - this was carried by the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodjenje - they said they were coming from Zvornik right then and the Serb forces had a quite a few casualties and quite a few wounded men and that the Muslim forces had 15 wounded and one casualty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that could not have been clear to me because by then I was already in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All of this that was carried by Oslobodjenje, is it in accordance with the facts that you had at your disposal at the time? They say the Serb forces had quite a few persons killed and wounded; the Muslims have one casualty. This conflict had broken out; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict had broken out, but I think that was a lie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean "lie"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not that many. Not that many Serbs were killed. Perhaps they were just alluding to something that they wanted to become part of the propaganda with which they would go into the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think? How many Serbs were killed in the conflict then, in this conflict that was started by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who started the conflict I don't know, but I know that in town two persons were killed, two Serbs who were at home, and Luka Radovic was killed who did take part in the fighting. I don't know about the others because I was arrested in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The two Serbs who were at home, I assume they did not attack anyone; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But they were killed by Arkan's people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Latus [phoen] was quite simply found in his apartment when they were searching all the apartments in Zvornik and looting them. He was my next-door neighbour. And beforehand, he had had open-heart surgery, I think it was in the States or somewhere. The man was ill, he could not leave his home. And as for Madam Nada, he wanted to protect two neighbours of hers, Futovic Taib and his son. They were killed on that day. She thought that through her own authority she could prove that they were honest men, but these people did not listen to anyone so she was killed in front of her house too. That's the only thing that I heard and that I know. That's all. I don't know about any other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about any other cases? Then we're going to move on to a different topic. Is it correct, Mr. 1524, that at the first multi-party elections held in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of municipality of Zvornik the SDS won?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The SDS. And the next party in line was the SDA, so they shared power in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, then, because the Serbs won in the multi-party elections, the first multi-party elections that were held in Bosnia-Herzegovina, why would the Serbs forcibly take over power in Zvornik when they had one power through the elections? As a person from Zvornik, although you were not born there but you lived there for decades, I believe that you could assist with that matter, in explaining this matter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the elections, power was shared on a reciprocal basis, depending on the number of votes won. This was quite all right. It was legal. What was not right was the way in which they shared power, both sides, the first few days. They simply barged into the committee building or, rather, the social political organisation's building, and they simply threw everyone out, not asking who were mere employees, staff members, and who were politicians. But in the time that preceded the war, there was a sharing of power, and during the last few months, it was said and it was somehow agreed quite simply that Zvornik, the town itself with the majority Muslim population should belong to the Muslims or, rather, that they would not cede it without a war most probably. On the other hand, the Serbs already had a vision that perhaps in the area of Celopek they could build some institutions of their own, a municipality, a bank for starters, where they could live and work. So what was being worked for was a division, a peaceful division, but that's not what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were they working for that, on this division? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were probably receiving instructions from higher places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I simplify matters, did I understand you correctly, when they won the elections, both the SDS and the SDA together, first threw out the communists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They considered them to be the common political enemy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Irrespective of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they fought between themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not fight. For about a year or so, they co-existed on the basis of tolerance. They even shared the communal buildings. The president of the municipality was a Muslim, the deputy was a Serb. The head of the SUP was a Muslim, the commander of the police was a Serb. What I'm saying is that it was quite normal. It was a tolerable political situation. However, on the other hand, the people who came in were not that capable. They were less capable from a political point of view, if I can put it that way, and in every other way. So they were not really up to the offices they held. Quite simply, it was the party leaders who were giving jobs in high places to people around them, their cronies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your assessment that these people in high places were for the most part not capable of performing these jobs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the people who left were people who were working for years, perhaps even decades, on their jobs very professionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe this is an important point by way of explanation. Now, let's move on to something else. You say that in June 1991, at the invitation of Grujic -- and it says here that he was president of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you went to a meeting so that you could explain your position there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not how I could explain my position, it was how -- for Grujic to explain what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, you're talking about June 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had to do with party affiliation. I wanted to leave the party because of some of the things that had happened previously within the party itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were elected to a high office in the party in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the leading positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the month of June 1991, you went to explain your position to them. You wanted to explain that you were no longer willing to carry on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the reasons? What motivated you to act that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, my very own position. Politically speaking, it differed from the position espoused by the leading people at the SDS at the time. Can I explain this in a bit more detail? Our offices were right opposite each other. There was only a wall between us, the SDA and the SDS. There were rumours, there was whispering at meetings so that the other side could not hear what was being said at meetings and what was being agreed upon, especially when the war broke out in Croatia. So this atmosphere at the meetings and outside the meetings was quite unbearable. And also apart from that, Grujic had already risen to the ranks of a leader who was deciding on everything. He is the one who made decisions. He's the one who went to meetings with the authorities of the SDS at republican level, and he also went elsewhere. He only gave others the information he was willing to share, but what he was not willing to share he did not share, and it was as simple as that. He was not really up to the high office he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you've been saying just now, I assume that you felt manipulated. He reported to you what he wanted to report about, and he presented pictures the way he wanted to present them, and he was the only one who was in touch with the higher leadership; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not consider that to be fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to explain your position. You wanted to say that you no longer wished to hold this position.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I and another friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this friend, did he also hold a high position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the Executive Committee of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you went to this meeting armed with a pistol because, as you say, you were afraid that somebody might attack you and even kill you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that there were certain telephone calls that I received that could lead me to think that, that all sorts of things could happen. Already by then Brano Grujic and a few other persons had declared themselves as people who could do anything and who could allow themselves to do all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was somebody killed? Before that and by then was somebody killed? How did this kind of thought cross your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few people were, and I didn't really want to give anyone the opportunity to do that to me too. At least I wanted to try to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody else armed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody attack you in any conceivable way, physically speaking? I'm going to explain why I'm putting this question to you. According to your statement, you said at that meeting that you did not want anything to do with thieves, and you left the meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you some kind of an explanation? Were they really thieves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, but those who I meant were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me so that I could at least get an impression as to what was going on. Since you called them thieves, does that mean that before that they had stolen something, or perhaps did they mobilise into the party leadership some persons who had had a criminal record or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some persons had had criminal records, and also some of them were involved in embezzlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of them who were there had embezzled some money; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who had embezzled some money, and whose money was it in the first place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Government money. The best thing for you would be to ask Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not have the opportunity of asking Brano Grujic because you are the person who is testifying here, not him. So that's why I'm asking you. Did he embezzle any money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, he did, and even much more later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which office did he hold when he embezzled the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he did not hold any particular office. At that time, he worked in a shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh. So he embezzled money in a shop that he worked in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that when you said you wouldn't have anything to do with thieves and you left? Nobody invited you to attend meetings any more, but nobody mistreated you in any way either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't invited to attend meetings, but they did call me up frequently on the phone at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They telephoned you using your home telephone number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they would make threats. And I reported this on one occasion to the post office. It wasn't out of fear, because they couldn't have protected me anyway, but I wanted to find out the numbers they were calling from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they rang you up and made anonymous phone calls and threats and things of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They insulted me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, they insulted you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were no consequences of that, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences came later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 of your statement you say that sometime in 1992, before the attack on Bijeljina - and you say you think it was the end of February as you say in your statement - you attended a meeting where a certain major was present by the name of Major Zoran Jovanovic, and as you say, he was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, along with two other officers from the Tuzla Corps. One of them was a captain by rank, and the other man was Lieutenant Sekanic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that after this meeting or before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, it was seven or eight months after the previous meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they did invite you to attend meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, but not before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how come you were invited to attend that particular meeting at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it turned out. That's what happened. I don't know how it happened and who decided to make the move, but Zoran Jovanovic phoned me personally and invited me to come to the meeting. And prior to that, I had met him in a coffee bar, and he said that preparations were under way, as he said at the time, that both sides were preparing themselves for a defence, to defend themselves from the other side and that all the officers would be necessary, reserve officers, that they should all take part and that it would be a good thing if I attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he explained to you that they were preparing to set up a defence because they assumed they would be attacked. You yourself were a reserve officer, and he was inviting you to attend the meeting in your capacity of reserve officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that before the attack on Bijeljina took place, sometime before the end of February, what kind of attack on Bijeljina are you referring to? What attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the time when Arkan's men, Arkan and his guys stormed into town and when the incidents that both I and I assume you remember very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, all right, you remember these incidents. I assume you remember them because you lived there. But tell me this: How did the first clashes and conflicts come about in the Bijeljina municipality? Because you remember them whereas I don't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I what I know is concerned, I learned it from state television, the state television programmes and their broadcasts, and all of us know about that. I remember it very well myself. Now, I don't know the particulars and what led up to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is it true that the conflicts took place at the end of March and beginning of April 1992? Which means quite some time after that meeting of yours took place where you were invited to attend as a reserve officer, according to my information.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when they called me up. Now, whether that was before or afterwards, I really don't know, and I don't think it's got anything to do with the events that took place in Bijeljina, because two or three months prior to the main conflict, both sides began to prepare themselves for war, to arm themselves and to establish some sort of -- well, not some sort of, but units in fact, made up of their own ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that same paragraph, paragraph 11, you go on to say that the Muslims, when they saw that there was -- that war was imminent, they began preparing themselves too, to arm themselves and so on, but all that had taken place much earlier, according to your descriptions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody knew about that in Bosnia-Herzegovina when the preparations started and when people began to arm themselves secretly, when the truckloads of ammunition were being driven in and weapons and so on, in some sort of illegal clandestine way. Both sides were busy arming themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, who up until the beginning of the conflicts was the president of the municipal Assembly in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Abdulah Pasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Osman Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably that kind of information can be found. Maybe it was, by I know the other two for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that through the mobilisation of the Muslim militia in Zvornik they ordered the president of the municipality and Abdulah Pasic, the deputy, and Nedzad Pasic, commander of the brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that that's who was involved? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it is right. Now, as to the order itself, I don't know anything about that order. I didn't know then and I don't know now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Sead Hadziavdic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name seems familiar, but I can't seem to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the proprietor of the Rojal coffee bar from Drinjaca, and according to my reports and police reports dating from the autumn of 1991, he was engaged in clandestinely arming the Muslims of the area. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know that they were arming themselves. Now, during what period and when exactly and the details of that, I don't know, but I do know that they were armed, as I say, at the beginning of the year and that they did possess weapons. Not only pistols which were sort of sidearms but automatic weapons as well, which meant that somebody was supplying them with arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know what this man Hadziavdic was doing, that the same thing was going on in Kamenica by Saban Desic [phoen] and Nedzad Haskic? Do their names seem familiar and do you know anything about their activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. Saban is now the president of the municipality of Zvornik. At the time he was an inspector, a trade inspector in Zvornik. So yes, people were arming themselves in all the villages, but who was personally responsible I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you at least know the role played in this arming and military organisation of the Zvornik Muslims by Captain Hajrudin Mesic, for instance, who was the former commander of the police station in Ugljevik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of that name, but quite possibly it was, although I don't know about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, since you yourself were probably very well-informed with what was going on in the area, from what you say, that one of the reasons for the evacuation of the Serbs from town - and you mentioned that many people did leave town - that this took place in January 1992 because a paramilitary unit named the Mosque Doves was formed led by a Zvornik criminal by the name of Mithad Grahic. Is that true? Is that the reason they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether that particular unit was established then or not, I really can't say. I have heard about certain groups. I did hear of the various groups, but what they were called I really don't know. I do know this man Midhat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a criminal, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in prison. Why he was in prison, I really can't say. He didn't belong to the circle of people I socialised with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't socialise with criminals, I assume, so you wouldn't know. But do you know during that during that period time in the wider region around Zvornik another Muslim paramilitary unit was set up called the Kobras, and the commander was a certain man called Suljo who before the war worked as a teacher in the village of Sapna, and it is assumed that it was actually Sulejman Terzic? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that was in the area of Sapna, that's quite a long way away, some 20 kilometres away. But as I say, there were rumours that a unit was being established and that people were standing guard. Even one of their men, a Muslim man, was killed, who had worked in Belgrade. He was coming back at night from Belgrade. He was going home. He didn't know about these watches that were being set up, and he was killed. And that was along that axis in that general direction of Grbavica in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Killed by the Muslim guards and watches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So there were watches, there were guards set up, they were armed, and everybody will tell you the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know anything about this unit called Kobra? Because later on it was commanded by Semsudin Mumerovic [phoen] whose nickname was Kobra who was later commander of the Zvornik Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was already in Holland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I'm not going to ask you any more about that. Now, have you heard of the events of March 1992 which caused a great deal of unrest amongst the Serbs when without any cause an ambush was set up and five people were arrested, five young Serb men, and they were interrogated by a man called Avdija Omerovic? And this took place in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably it did, but as I say, information was coming in less frequently because everybody was doing their best to save their own skin and save their own lives at the time. So maybe that's quite true, but it just passed me by and perhaps I didn't pay much attention to it or perhaps I didn't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But at any rate, you can't remember so I don't want to pursue that point any further. But in paragraph 11, you say that it was precisely this man Abdulah Music who showed you a box of automatic and semi-automatic rifles which the Muslim side had procured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was on the eve of Bajram, the Bajram festival on the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he told you that he had bought it from some Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you claim that the Serbs were preparing to attack the Muslims, whereas at the same time they were actually selling them rifles, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything is possible. If those same people could have sold flour when there was a ban on flour -- they did this from Serbia and trucks would bring the flour in and reload it onto other trucks going to Tuzla and so on -- if this could be procured by the Serbs and sold to the Muslims, then why shouldn't the same people sell weapons and arms? Nothing strange there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I assume there's some difference between flour and weapons. I understand that people are bringing in flour on the black market and selling it, but I'm asking you about arms, weapons. How is it possible that if the Serbs were preparing themselves for an armed conflict, that they would at the same time be selling arms to the side that they were allegedly to go into conflict with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those same people sold arms to the Serbs as well. One automatic rifle would cost you 1.200 German marks, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So these were black marketeers selling weapons to anybody, anybody they could sell them too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't anybody doing this in an organised fashion or organised arming or an organised Serb formation collecting weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, far from it. Individuals engaged in that kind of thing. You can't speak of the entire population or any legal units, lawful units doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's a very essential point. Now, you also said that at the meeting held with respect to the Zvornik unit, that Grujic, Dragan Spasojevic, and Sveto Popovic had the main say. They were the main speakers at the meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, yes, those three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all three men were people who were from Zvornik themselves, and they held posts and positions in Zvornik and had done so for many years; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not for many years. They were -- nobody had ever heard of them. They were anonymous citizens before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, what I meant was that they were from Zvornik and had lived in Zvornik for many years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They lived in Zvornik for a long time, many years, except this man Sveto Popovic, Sveto Popovic. The others were from a village from the Zvornik municipality. Grujic himself was born in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but he lived in Zvornik for a long time, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that all three men were inhabitants and residents of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had been that for at least 20 years.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that they hadn't come in from anywhere, from Serbia or from where else. They hadn't come in to Zvornik during that period of time; they'd been living there as residents for 20-odd years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also say that Major Zoran Jovanovic was commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed to that position before the war broke out. That's what he said. He would say he was commander for the Zvornik municipality. Now, what he actually was and what that was at that time establishment-wise, I can't say. Whether it was a brigade or a form of Territorial Defence or something else, I really can't say, but they were people who at all events were members of something above a battalion. So if they were commanders of battalions or companies or something specific, and he was their commander, then the next step up the ladder in that kind of hierarchy was a brigade commander, going up the chain of command that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've forgotten your number, Witness. Yes, Mr. 1524. That's all I wanted to establish. What it was was a meeting where these units were being formed, the inception of those units was discussed at the meeting. Because you yourself said that you were making the logical conclusion that if battalions had been formed that it should have been a brigade. But it was a meeting, and the brigade hadn't actually been established yet. It was in the process of being established through that meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they had appointed commanders and if they had lists, each commander had lists of his members belonging to his unit, and this was uni-ethnic, uni-national, then the unit was being established although not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but as I say, it was the local Territorial Defence and your joint organisation and deployment and distribution of the members of that local Territorial Defence into those units of the Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say major, commander of the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for one minute to tell you that you have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm very sorry to hear that, Mr. May. I wasn't watching the clock. This witness is providing some very interesting testimony, so could you at least give me a little more time and I'll do my best to skip over some of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will have ten minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me skip over this part. That is to say, you had this particular office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is written here, and I'm not going to refer to it specifically so that you won't be identified, and then you say the unit consisted of local volunteers, members of the TO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some had voluntarily joined up by then. They asked to be armed. They asked to be among the ranks of the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this was the local Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in paragraph 14, you say that the Zvornik Brigade, that Zvornik Brigade, your unit of Territorial Defence that you established from the ranks of the local population in Zvornik. It's your brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it had a total of 3 to 4.000 members, as it says here. Let's not go into all of that. Was that approximately the manpower involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even a bit more. Not straight away, but as the war went on, certainly it involved a lot more people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even had some tanks, and the tank crews were made up of reservists from Zvornik as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't some tanks. It was a tank company from Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the crews were made up of volunteers from Zvornik; is that right? That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now you say, in paragraph 15, that Serbs would go to various weekend cottages over the weekend, as people usually do, and some went across the Drina to Serbia, to Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's where the weekend cottages were for the most part because the area was more conducive to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the former Yugoslavia people did not pay attention to republican boundaries. People from Zvornik, that was a biggish town, had weekend cottages on the other side of the Drina River in the area of Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And most of them were Muslims, the people who had weekend cottages there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say since they had a premonition that something bad could happen over the weekend, then they sought shelter in these weekend cottages of theirs in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Some even took their furniture from their apartments there so that it would not be destroyed once the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Kozluk, villages around Zvornik, were visited by Grujic, Pasovic, and Muhamed Jelkic, a Muslim, just before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was director of the hospital. But I'm not aware of this visit and these meetings, no -- this visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that these three men, together with hodza Muhamed Efendi Ilugavica [phoen] and a Serb priest, Vasilije Kacavenda, went to see the people from Sepak and Kotici and asked them not to allow a conflict to break out and not to resort to force? You say they were asking them not to tear down barricades. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Kacavenda is the Bishop of Zvornik and Tuzla. I really don't know that anyone went there. And just before the conflict at that. Movement was already restricted for Serbs in Serb villages and for Muslims in Muslim villages. I doubt it. I don't think that on the very eve of the war anybody would have gone. The commander of the police went, though. He went towards Kula. He was a Serb. And he was killed. So I doubt it. I doubt the possibility of this kind of walking around villages and trying to talk people into doing this or that. It would have been very easy for them to get killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wrote this down here and I found it in your statement, but I don't have time to look through the statement now, but that can readily be established. You say in paragraph 16 that from people from the newly established brigade you found out that there would be attack on Zvornik. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a week earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 18 that the Serbs on the 5th or 6th of April started bringing up barricades on Vidakovoj Njivi.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if people are putting up barricades on a field, and this is Vidak's field, Vidakovoj Njivi, does it mean that they were defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a real field. This is just a place called Vidakovoj Njivi and this is on the outskirts of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, isn't that something that is done by way of defence rather than by way of attacking a town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be used for both, depending on which side of the barricade you're on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In the same paragraph, you say that that night, with people of both ethnic groups, you organised within your own building some kind of a watch, and you were trying to follow everything that was going on, everything that was happening to Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody was together in the town until the shooting broke out, and then when the shooting broke out, a minority went towards Kula Grad and the majority, Muslims and Serbs, crossed over to Mali Zvornik in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that you wanted to cross over the bridge to Mali Zvornik but it was held by Muslim forces. They held it under their control and they did not allow anyone to cross the bridge. That's what you say in paragraph 23; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just before the attack, just before the attack. It was Wednesday morning. They did not allow people to get out of buildings, and they used a bus and also a truck to set up a roadblock not allowing people to leave, because they were afraid that if Serbs left town, they would be left as the only target, but this way they were both there and then God would allow things to happen one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please be brief. They did not allow you to cross the bridge, the Muslim forces did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the Serb side it was the Serbs, and on the Muslim side it was the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that on the side of the Republic of Serbia there was only the police. Nobody else could have been there. Tell me you recognised an Albanian, Dzavid Behljuji, and a certain Ibrahimovic and some other people there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the three of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all three were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a conflict, so it was not an attack of the Serbs on the town of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing had happened by then. Nothing had broken out. There were only watches and guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that in the evening of the 8th of April, as the conflicts were abating, a large number of people, 10.000 people, left Zvornik and went to Serbia via Mali Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among those 10.000 who fled from Zvornik, they fled because the conflict had broken out in Zvornik. 10.000 people fled to Serbia. They were Muslims and Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, more of them were Muslims because there were more Muslims among the population of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so more of them were going to Serbia because they wanted to seek shelter there as they knew that it was safe in Serbia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the conflict broke out in Zvornik and the Muslims, as you said just now, were fleeing to Serbia, seeking shelter there. It was quite clear to them this was not a conflict that came from Serbia, this was a local conflict between the Serbs and Muslims in Zvornik; isn't that right? And they were going to Serbia where it was safe, to seek shelter there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. 99.9 per cent of the people who went to Serbia were saved persons. This .01 [as interpreted] per cent were arrested in Serbia and returned. That would be about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right if it's my last question. This 0.01 [as interpreted] per cent that were arrested somewhere in Serbia, it was your forces in Mali Zvornik who arrested them; right? They were not arrested by the forces of the Serb police or anybody else. It was your forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested by the Serb police, I for one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And without any kind of procedure, any kind of preliminary procedure that is customary in the civilised world, they simply sent me back to the camp in Alhos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did they arrest you at the request of the Zvornik authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any kind of request. They had no request. They simply arrested me in the street as if I were a criminal, with three or four cars, police cars. They surrounded me, arrested me, threw me into the car and handed me over in Bosnia, in Zvornik, to Brane Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time now is more than up. You've had more than sufficient time, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we just finish the subject that was just started? I would like to deal with that only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, out of these 10.000 people who decided to go to Serbia, among them were there people from Zvornik? And Zvornik is in Bosnia, and Mali Zvornik is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these 10.000 people, they went to Serbia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there people who went towards the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina during those days or was it for the most part this wave that went to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that perhaps 2 or 3.000 went towards Bosnia, towards Kula Grad. It's also there on the border, the Zvornik municipality, but from there people could go to Central Bosnia, but most of the inhabitants of Zvornik, the town of Zvornik which had a population that was about 80 per cent Muslim, went to Mali Zvornik, to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. However, when you arrived in Banja Koviljaca, as you said in paragraph 47, that is far into Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that there you saw about 1.000 Muslims. Were they taken care of in Banja Koviljaca or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than a thousand. They went individually to the houses of their friends. People socialised even before the war. All the hotels were full. They took rooms in hotels legally. Nobody prevented them from doing that. They paid for it. It was full. The town of Loznica was full. The park was full. It wasn't a thousand, it was several thousand Muslims who were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any Muslims go voluntarily to other countries in Europe on the basis of an organisation that was provided by the international community like it was made possible for you to go to another country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not made possible for me. I went to another country in another way, but I heard here, because I do socialise with people, that it was made possible for them to move on. I was even present in Belgrade when two families were given passports. They had not had passports, and they were given passports at the Belgrade SUP so they could travel legally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just give me an answer to one more question so that the Judges would be aware of that. You mentioned black uniforms yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before all of these things that happened, or perhaps after all of these things that happened, did you ever see a single soldier of the Yugoslav army or of the army of Yugoslavia in a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may with your permission, just ask Witness B-1524 a couple of questions in re-examination. Re-examined by Mr. Agha:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-1524, you mention that before the attack on Zvornik the SDA and SDS were trying to negotiate things peacefully. Can you tell me, please, which body or which group actually attacked Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I said this by way of a joke, but that is indeed true, as Mr. Milosevic noted. I always say that some people talk about the defence of Zvornik and others talk about the attack on Zvornik. So regardless of terminology, I know that on the previous day Arkan's soldiers and Arkan himself were already in Karakaj, and on that previous day, four or five of them were arrested in Zvornik in a Mercedes that was full of weapons. In addition to these local people who took part in the attack, it was Arkan's units that participated in the attack. These were the men who were in black uniforms. These were the men who looted the town, who committed a series of crimes, murders within the town itself. These were not JNA units. These were no legal units. These were paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Witness, could you please tell the Court where Arkan and his units came from, from which republic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan has a house in Belgrade. He had one before the war. He was a Belgrader. These people who were questioning me after my arrest, who were down there in Alhos, spoke with a Belgrade accent. It's no secret. People know that, and people know where Arkan recruited his men, from the urban population, and there were a number of Belgraders within his ranks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one final question: You mentioned that when you were in Mali Zvornik after the attack or the defence, however you call it, there was shelling coming from Mali Zvornik in Serbia. Can you kindly tell the Chamber who was carrying out this shelling of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1524 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this, but they told me that this was coming from an elevation above Mali Zvornik. A mortar unit was there, and it consisted of men from Zvornik, members of the Territorial Defence of Zvornik only. They were up there at that elevation so that they could have a good view and that they could carry out their task properly. They were perhaps a kilometre away from the Drina as the crow flies, on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So actually, Witness, one lead-on question from that: If that mortar battery was placed about one kilometre on the Serbian side, would it be your impression that it was a pre-arranged attack or defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can really answer that. He can -- all he can say is this: Did you see any signs of an arrangement before any attack as to arrangements being made for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if at the very moment when they were shooting -- I mean, the units would have had to have been deployed there for a day or two before that. They would have had to have positioned themselves in order to be able to target various areas. So that unit must have been there at that elevation a day or two before the shooting actually took place. It's not only this mortar unit. They were shooting above our heads. We were in Mali Zvornik, and sub-machine-guns were used for that. And also there were these other hills in the area, and the Bosnian side was targeted from those hills too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And that completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B-1524, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. Would you just wait while the blinds are pulled down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before the next witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- mention a couple of administrative matters concerning his evidence. I trust the Chamber will have received the replacement and final signed version of his statement. There were some variations as I set out in a memorandum. Inevitably, as I forecast, there were amendments. I hope they haven't been inconvenient for the Chamber. Our interpretation of the ruling as to which passages should be given live and in full is set out in the memorandum, and I hope that we've got the paragraph numbers correct. We've tended not to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It inevitably causes inconvenience when there are last-minute changes to statements, that must be said, and it is a practice which should be avoided, clearly, as far as possible. Not only is the Chamber inconvenienced but also, of course, all those others working on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say that from the beginning I explained that this was a draft and why it could only be a draft, the witness coming here in the circumstances he was and so on, and indeed I raised the matter on a couple of subsequent occasions thinking it clear that there would inevitably be changes in the manner in which his evidence could be given. In any event, my calculation is that the passages that the Chamber wishes to be given live and in full are paragraphs 98 to 109, 119 and 120, and 124 to the end, and I hope that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. One thing I note is that most of the changes are in fact favourable to the cross-examiner, putting it neutrally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Such clarifications as there have been have helped the Defence. But looking to the future -- we obviously have to consider this position, but looking to the future, we must try and work out a way in which this matter can be dealt with in a way which is more expeditious and fairer for all concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a particular type of witness, as I've explained for several months, and as you know, perhaps -- perhaps can we just have a short private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received this, Mr. May. As a matter of fact, I received it last night.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This version that Mr. Nice referred to, I received it last night. That was the first time I could receive it, because my associate and I had a meeting that was planned for 6:00 p.m. That's when I got it. As for this practice that Mr. Nice has of providing me with material at the very last moment, I asked you on several occasions to do away with this kind of practice. There was this rule that material should be provided a month in advance, and you shortened it to ten days, but Mr. Nice has not even honoured that decision that I be provided with material ten days in advance. Sometimes he provides me with certain papers only ten minutes in advance. So I don't want to deal with anything specific in relation to this witness - I'm going to question every witness - but I ask that out of sheer decency I get all these materials at least ten days in advance, as you had prescribed. I'm saying this for the sake of the future. I don't want to interrupt your plan in any way now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We make it plain that it is not the Court's plan that these statements should arrive at the last moment, and it's a matter of concern to the Trial Chamber that you should have adequate time. We, too, received that new version at 5.00 last night, and as you've heard me raise with the Prosecution, that in the normal course of events is going to be insufficient time. However, we've looked at these particular amendments. They are all, as far as I can see, favourable to you, and therefore, we don't think it right -- or I don't think it right to keep them out. But I suggest that we use the new version for that reason. However, in the future, we will most certainly have in mind this question of time, because plainly you must have the time in order to prepare your cross-examination, and that's a matter we're conscious of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And may I say that any time that you need to have, as a result of the late arrival of the documents from the Prosecution, should be taken from the Prosecution's overall time. I'd just like to endorse what the Presiding Judge has said. The practice is quite unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I, because I think it's appropriate and indeed necessary that I should do so, explain the practical difficulties which I'm sure are not always immediately apparent. If you have a witness like this coming to court in the circumstances he does, and the Court knows about that, we can only deal with him when he's here. Preparing these documents, especially to prepare them in two languages, is an enormously difficult exercise involving a large number of people. The material from which this statement was taken has of course been available to the accused for years. He's been notified of the calling of this witness for a considerable period of time, and the books have all been available to him, and it is from the books, and to a limited degree from the witness -- from the interview of the witness, that the material has been drawn. The only way that we could avoid it with this type of witness this type of situation is by calling him here a fortnight or a month before and keeping him here. We couldn't do that. It's not possible. So sorry. As to the particular statements, the position is that I provided you with a draft at the earliest conceivable moment, a draft that had been prepared in forecast of what we would want from the witness, knowing of the books that he'd written, alerting everyone to the fact that it was a draft on a couple of occasions last week, and I have the references that I made to that. The Prosecution worked from last Tuesday through to last Sunday afternoon and the version was signed by the witness Sunday afternoon, he then being content with it. It was made available to the Chamber first thing on Monday morning but a red-line version was wanted and Ms. Dicklich worked on that all day and it was provided later in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
