utterances.text: And very helpful it was too, but Mr. Nice, you have to appreciate that there are others in this trial besides the Prosecution whose interests have to be taken account of. That includes the Trial Chamber. And if documents arrive at the last moment, we may have to simply adjourn as being the only way that we can deal with it, and the accused by -- in fairness to him, can deal with it too, and that would be time which will have to be taken off your budget. But in any event, the matter does not arise now but let us hope that it doesn't arise in future. Let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go ahead on the new version. If you want more time, of course you can have it, but it will come off the rest of the week, that's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will not be surprised to know that the six hours allocated for cross-examination, given the inclusion of favourable parts within the statement served, is a matter we have very much in mind. I'm simply going to do my best in the circumstances, but I am very anxious, and I know we've exhausted the topic and I'll -- but I'm very anxious that the Chamber should appreciate that I'm doing everything I can to bring material before this Chamber that is helpful and is timely, and there are simply circumstances which are beyond better organisation save by quite exponential enlargement of costs and labour, which we can't afford. We simply cannot have witnesses here for months or have people away from the office proofing them for weeks on end. It isn't possible. We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check one thing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was this translated, the last version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I've introduced the following system. You might like to know the practicalities of how we do this. If you have a witness who is giving a statement, typically it's given in one language and then the thing is translated by the Language Services, and that takes weeks to do it typically, because there is no overnight facility for translation of any substantial document, and there couldn't be for us or for the Chamber or the Registry without huge expense. So what we now do is we have two interpreters or language assistants working with any witness so that as a document is being drawn or amended in the language of the interview, which will be typically English, there's somebody working in parallel preparing or amending the document so that it's available pretty well instantaneously in B/C/S, and that's the way we are able now to serve the rule change under 89 to provide documents in both languages. But it has represented a substantial increase in resource allocation which we've negotiated with Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will continue after the adjournment with the witness on the new version. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your full name, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I'm going to summarise your dealings with the Office of the Prosecutor in order to identify the materials with which we are working. But first by way of background, born in October 1928, holding various offices, government offices in your career, mostly in social and economic development, and being ambassador to Italy in the mid to late 1970s. Were you, in March 1989, elected as Serbia's representative to the SFRY Presidency, the vice-president of that Presidency from the 15th of May, 1989 to the 15th of May, 1990, president from the 15th of May 1990 to the 15th of May, 1991? Following that were you president of the Socialist Party of Serbia from the 24th of May of 1991 until the 24th of October, 1992, taking over from the accused who had at that time had to step down. When he returned to the leadership of the party, did you become vice-president of the party again, holding that position until November of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With that much background, is the position that you have written two books, one called "The Last Days of the SFRY, A Diary," and the second book, the Book on Milosevic? Have you also been interviewed as a suspect by officers of the OTP on three occasions, in September 2002 and in April and September of 2003? Did you thereafter come to The Hague pursuant to a subpoena and have you engaged in what are called proofing sessions with the Office of the Prosecutor from last Tuesday or Wednesday and until the end of this weekend?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of those proofing sessions, which themselves drew on the books and the interview but particularly on the books, were you in a position to sign a statement yesterday afternoon of 40 pages in English and a slightly different number in B/C/S, and was that statement an accurate statement of events?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you indeed have a copy of the B/C/S version of that statement for reference purposes if appropriate and if required?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as your diary is concerned, and you understand that it was for the production of your diary that the Office of the Prosecutor sought your assistance, so far as the diary is concerned, is that a document that the book called The Diary, is that a document prepared on contemporaneous notes?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are notes which have not been edited or redacted. They have been printed as they were taken down in note form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does your diary, paragraph 5 of the statement, set out something in excess of a hundred meetings or conversations you had with the accused between May 1989 and July 1992, frequently being meetings you attended with five other people, or up to five other people, the overall group being described by you as the six and the composition of that group being the accused, Kadijevic, Adzic, Kostic, and Bulatovic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the other conversations these two were recorded, and that group of people I entitled the group of six, the six, for it -- to facilitate matters in my diary so that I needn't go through all the six names. But it never had the formal title of "the six."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to your offices, you stood down as president to be replaced by Stipe Mesic in 1990 -- 1991. The Rump Presidency with which we are familiar, did you remain a member of the Rump Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Until the creation of the new Yugoslavia, which was sometime around the 15th of May, 1992, however, in formal terms we worked a little longer, until the new president of the state was elected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your diary as a book was published in 1995, and you were immediately dismissed by the accused. He demanded your resignation from office of member of parliament which you then held. You complied immediately with his request. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: As far as this replacement was concerned in the party leadership, I never received an explanation of the reasons why that came about, but indirectly, I was told that it was because of the book. Now, as far as the position held in the Federal Assembly of the deputy mandate there, I was asked to tender my resignation, and I accepted that because I knew that it would be put into practice even if I didn't want it to be. So to avoid any unnecessary complication, it was far simpler for me to do that myself. And the procedure was fairly simple, according to the rules and procedure --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Who would have put it into practice had you declined to comply with the accused's request?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: It would have been put into practice by the party itself. It would have excluded me from the party membership, the leadership of the party, I mean, and this would lead to a situation in which I had no right to be on the list of the Socialist Party and then the Socialist Party would report to the national Assembly who the next man on the electoral list was who had not become a deputy yet but who would be a replacement for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you say in paragraph 6 of your statement in respect of resigning as a member of parliament: "I agreed to do it immediately, because I knew that if I did not agree, he would arrange for it to be done." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was convinced that that was how things would turn out. And I'm sure they would have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your second book, the Book on Milosevic published some five years later, focuses on the accused as an individual. You say in paragraph 7 of your statement -- perhaps I ought to deal with exhibiting the statement and all the other documents in a second but if I can deal with this first question and then get on with that. You say that the accused was the key figure and the main actor in the Serbian tragedy that you describe. Is that your opinion still?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, for more than a decade, Milosevic was the main political figure in Serbia. He held absolute authority within the people and within the party, and he had the possibility of having a decisive role on all decisions made. And by the same token, he was in a way the main actor of everything that came to pass during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the statement of the witness, under 89(F), be exhibited, and may the file of exhibits be comprehensively linked with it so that the statement becomes the first tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got three binders here. Let's get them right. I have got exhibits, and then there is at the beginning of that page a list of contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second binder and third binder are simply tabs 2 and 3, which are the books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tab 2 and 3. So the statement and the exhibits can all have a single exhibit number then. We'll have the next number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit number is 596.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement to which I have been referring is 596, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you make the point in respect of both your books, at paragraph 8, that you completely stand by what is written in them and you believe them to be an accurate source of historical material for the ICTY but you accept that so far as personal views and judgements are concerned they are entirely that, personal views, and they may, of course, be open to question.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the facts are concerned, the ones presented in the books, they were recorded exactly as I saw them. So I consider them to be historical facts. Now, as far as my assessments go, and judgements, they can always be questioned because that is my personal assessment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to evidence in some detail and just to complete the picture of your dealings with the Office of the Prosecutor, in the course of your time here last week, have you been shown and have you had a chance to review several exhibits which are now contained in the binder before the learned Judges?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibits I have looked through, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed one or two exhibits were even shown to you this morning, they coming to attention late?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been notified in general terms of some other supplementary questions that you may be asked in respect of topics covered in the statement, those matters being raised at a late stage and too late for inclusion in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you understand, Mr. Jovic, that whereas much of your evidence will be taken in chief from the witness statement itself, there are passages that we must deal with in detail and I now turn to those, although they will be slightly out of order chronologically but to ensure that they are covered in the detail the Chamber requires. So in the English version of the statement, I go to page 27, and for you, Mr. Jovic, if you want to find it, and with the Chamber's leave, if you could have it open, we're dealing at paragraph 97 and thereabouts. Before I come to the paragraphs that we have to deal with specifically but in order to give chronological context -- and this is a document, Your Honour, we may not need to look at, but I can refer to -- tab 19, on the 7th of October, 1991, was there a decision to promote Mladic from colonel to general of which you are aware, Mr. Jovic? A decision made by the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I was shown the text of those minutes from the Presidency meeting, and I said during the proofing sessions, and I state again, that I don't remember that, although quite obviously I did attend that meeting. And that is for the simple reason that we had a series of other important questions on the agenda. And the last points of the agenda usually are prepared at a cadre's personnel commission or the commission for promotion and decorations and we never discussed these matters much at Presidency sessions. So I can't say that I remember the event taking place, but most probably what it says in the document is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again a document we needn't review save to the extent it's necessary for you to authenticate it; did you listen yesterday to an intercept, tab 17, said to have been the intercept of a telephone conversation between you and Karadzic on the 15th of October, 1991? Did you recognise the voices and do you accept that this is a telephone conversation between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did listen to that, and I do. Confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days later, on the 17th of October, at a conference here in The Hague, were you present?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we need this from you in some detail. What did Kostic tell you about Montenegro's attitude towards Lord Carrington's plan?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, we received, with great delay, a document which was supposed to have been considered here in The Hague in the coming days, and we did our best to study it and to assume positions. It was common knowledge that there was a difference between the proposal put forward by Lord Carrington and the positions assumed by us. The crux of those differences was that Lord Carrington's plan provided for the disbanding of Yugoslavia, whereby each republic could become independent on the basis of a referendum. We, however, considered that it was better and the right thing to do to write down that each republic may do so on the basis of a referendum by the people, a popular referendum of the people and nations, because in certain republics, there are many nationalities living there, and those who do not wish to step down from Yugoslavia can enjoy the right of staying within Yugoslavia. So we expected Montenegro to accept this too, the position that we held. However, Branko Kostic, when he just looked through the documents, said Montenegro will accept the proposal made by Lord Carrington. I didn't believe him. I thought that he was joking. And so once again, I asked him and cautioned him and said that this would be catastrophic for our overall policy, both Serbia and the Serbian people. And he said that he was informed that that would be done. And I then informed Milosevic about that, because I was going to see him anyway for us to have a look at Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 29135 to 29139. the document, to go through it and see what we were to do. And first of all, he didn't believe it. Then he tried to get hold of Bulatovic over the phone to talk to him, and it was not customary not to be able to reach Bulatovic, because they said he was otherwise engaged. That was unusual. Later on, we received a telefax from Montenegro saying precisely what Kostic had told me, and that's how that matter ended. Montenegro, at that point in time, had decided to accept the Carrington Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the next Presidency session of the PSFRY, you took the floor, and you dealt with the fact that Montenegro had taken this position, and your attitude was to do and to say what?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I took the floor and then I turned towards Kostic and said, "We're going to outvote you here today because there are more of us in favour of the position backed by Serbia." However, it turned out that Kostic thought the same. And although he was president in the Presidency, he did not accept Montenegro's position but, rather, accepted the position taken by the Yugoslav state Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are then a couple of exhibits I want you to deal with, because although we're taking this passage of your evidence slightly out of sequence, I want the exhibits to be dealt with within this passage of evidence chronologically. Tab 15, please. And if this could be simply laid on the overhead projector and I'll summarise its effect because the witness has seen it. Do you recall, Mr. Jovic, receiving on the 25th -- a document dated the 25th of October of 1991 from UNESCO, Frederico Mayor, setting out their interest in world heritage and natural heritage sites, and in particular in the city of Dubrovnik, proposing that a mission should be sent to your country in view of what was happening and to recommend measures to be taken to ensure the protection of, amongst other things, Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't remember the document previously, but I see that it is indeed true, and I responded and said that they could come and that we would allow them to conduct an on-site investigation. So I think that the document is authentic and that we did let them go ahead with what they planned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We come back in the bundle of exhibits to tab 5, and there are two versions of this document. Was there something called a Supreme Command meeting held on the 26th of October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could lay the English version of this - and the witness has reviewed it - on the overhead projector, please, starting with the first page which sets out those who were present. We can see that yourself, you rather, Branko Kostic, Bajramovic, Jovo Kostic, Kadijevic and other Supreme Command Staff members were present. And if we turn then to the second page, at the foot of the page we see Mr. Kostic concluding that there should be the mobilisation of 220.000 additional conscripts. We go to the next page, please. We see your contribution as recorded in this minute. Next page, please. Thank you very much. No, sorry. The page before. My mistake. And where -- I can't see it on this. Sorry. There it is. That's it. Your contribution is as follows: "We have experience from previous mobilisations and the problem of not understanding the situation. The question is if we can allow our activities to depend on the success of mobilisation. I am very afraid that wanting too much may lead to a boomerang effect with catastrophic consequences. Do not think that it is up to one man, a politician. Thus the army must not observe just the numbers of this and that, but what it should do. I am afraid of mass resistance because the situation is not the same everywhere. Perhaps the best situation is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Unfortunately, it is hard to bring back the refugees, and another question is how things will proceed in Montenegro. "The people do not know if a new state with a new army will be created: Making a decision is an immense question. Much has occurred, from Slovenia to Croatia, problems have appeared, major goals and aspirations, which could not be achieved. There is much disparity between plans for mobilisation and what can actually be done. This is because mobilisation 2.5 times as extensive should be carried out." And then if we go over to SSNO Kadijevic: "I want to ensure that nobody among us wants to impose a political solution, but rather support and secure them militarily." Followed by Adzic saying, second line: "... regarding the Serb leadership's orientation for all Serbs to live in one state, or the orientation for any nation to live in Yugoslavia if it wants to." And I think if we go over, perhaps Kostic further down the page, saying: "I believe that the Montenegrin people are not in favour of the current decision of the Montenegrin Assembly. If the people, the Serbs in the Krajinas, are in favour of fighting for Yugoslavia, then it's very important that we know what we're going to fight for." And then finally over the page, please, Usher, to the foot of the next page where you, Mr. Jovic, are recorded as agreeing with Veljko Kadijevic. "Concerning the political situation, we need to know the following regarding the situation in Montenegro: Are we going to defend even those who do not want to go with us? We cannot change a concept building a state and army if Montenegro is against it. There will be a new international circumstance because Serbia would remain alone. I believe that the Montenegrin leadership doesn't understand that situation, because the following are the concepts: Either six states signing a cooperation agreements or two to three states in one. Our problem," you said, "currently is how to estimate the real prospect creating a bigger force, what we need to do is create such a force, within its possibilities. Thus it's very important to entrench unity on the political level and make it operational. That's why we need to clear this and confirm the level ..." There are two notes of this meeting but that's the one I've read from. Do you accept that this reflects your contribution to the meeting of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: This is a note. They are minutes which -- it is not a stenogram nor is it a verified minutes. It is the personal note-taking of somebody sitting in the room making notes for somebody else. And what I can do is to clarify the substance of the discussion. I cannot say that all this is correct as it happened, but there are certain elements there, yes. I don't think that this person recording these notes understood what was going on, but I was fully conscious of what was taking place. At that point in time, a problem had arisen between Serbia and Montenegro with respect to Carrington's plan, and also a sort of divergence of views came about between the leadership of Serbia and Montenegro with respect to their relationship towards the Serb question and towards Serbs living outside Serbia and outside Montenegro in general. And therefore, there was a problem of a lack of clarity, in what way Montenegro would behave toward the Yugoslav army and whether the Yugoslav army could exist until the problem had been resolved. So that was one aspect of the problem. The second aspect was this: The army demanded additional mobilisation of 220.000 or 250.000 men, conscripts, because all the fronts that it held allegedly it said it was not able to hold with the number of men it had at its disposal, and especially it was not able to withdraw and free people from the barracks that had been blocked in Croatia. And there were many barracks with very few men in them, but it was both a military and a political problem. Now, as far as the first question is concerned, the political relationship between Serbia and Montenegro, that was not able to be resolved at that meeting. It was a problem which would affect the further fate of the army and how -- what our attitude towards the army would be. So we expected this to be cleared up between Serbia and Montenegro, which was recorded in the notes later on and in my diary. Now, the call for mobilisation seems to be reflected here but not in precise terms. I said that we cannot accept, as the army seems to feel, that one politician, Milosevic or myself or both of us, could take a public stance and demand that the people respond to the mobilisation and that the mobilisation would succeed in rallying several thousand men. That is not something we can be expected to do or asked of us. And secondly, this requirement for over 200.000 men was a megalomaniac one and if we did ask for that many men it would have a boomerang effect and the citizens would quite simply not respond to the call-up for mobilisation and that we ought to be more realistic and to look at it in the lights of the realistic situation. And the conclusion was that nothing in fact could have -- be concluded but we ought to weigh up the questions with the republics first and see whether Serbia and Montenegro were prepared to live life together, to have that common concept and their relationship to the army and what the republics felt with respect to the proposed mobilisation. So that would be the substance of that conversation and meeting. And as I say, the notes and records and minutes are more of an aide-memoire. They're not very detailed and specific, and I cannot accept it as being a document or, rather, it can be a document to the effect that it says that the meeting did take place and the people who attended and a sort of indication of the general discussion held at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're pressed for time, but thank you for that detail on this occasion. On the 30th of October, was a text drawn up for Montenegro to send to The Hague? If so, by whom, and in very short order, what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, we had talks with the Montenegrin leadership. They promised that they would think about it a bit more. They returned home, and basically they agreed to change their position. Then there was a bit of a dispute in terms of whether this position would be proposed by Serbia and that they second it or whether it should be the other way round. Mr. Milosevic drafted the text. Basically it is one sentence. And he insisted that they should be the ones putting forth the proposal. Ultimately, they agreed to it, and they proposed the text, and Serbia accepted that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 103. Milosevic and Kadijevic, how did they get on at this time and in relation to this topic? Was there a meeting of the six at which Kadijevic and Adzic expressed a view contrary to the position you and Milosevic were taking? Paragraph 103.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. As for Adzic and Kadijevic, we did not discuss this with them as far as I can remember. We talked to the Montenegrins regarding the Carrington Plan. And then, after having finished the discussion with them, then we asked Kadijevic and Adzic to join in so that we discuss the questions of the military, the joint army, mobilisation, and other such issues. Of course they were kept abreast of what was going on, but this was not discussed with them. Now, if we're looking at The Diary, that's the way things were. So that's what happened at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You make a point, I think, in The Diary about Milosevic saying something about helping them abundantly. Do you remember that in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Which part of The Diary is this? Oh, I see. Well, look, this is an episode. It wasn't on that day. It wasn't at that time either. Just a moment, please. There was this one episode when they had objected to us, to Milosevic, that we no longer cared about the Serb people outside Serbia. Milosevic told them that that is not correct, that we always helped them and that we will continue to help them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're now coming to the period of November/December 1991. I want to put a few things in chronological order. First of all, at tab 18, not for detailed review for want of time, but have you reviewed another telephone intercept of a conversation between you and Karadzic said to have taken place on the 18th of November, tab 18?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They showed this to me and I listened to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the voices are yours and Karadzic's?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed that the conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- depending on time, I may come back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 23rd of November, there was a document that you've had a chance to consider, the Geneva Accord. It's already been produced. It's Exhibit 396, tab 6. So if we can just lay that on the overhead projector as appropriate. And as you appreciate, Mr. Jovic, my questions are directed, amongst other things, at the issue of the control by the Rump Presidency of the influence over, as might describe it, the army. And this is the Geneva Accord, introduced through the evidence of Mr. -- Ambassador, I beg your pardon, Okun. It's dated the 23rd of November, 1991. It's a document with which I think you are familiar, and we can see on the overhead projector that the accused, with Kadijevic and Vance perhaps as witness, agreed that Croatia would lift its blockade of barracks; B, that the JNA with immediate effect would begin with the withdrawal from Croatia of the personnel, weapons, and military equipment in those barracks installations, and complete this process in accordance with schedules; C, that they will instruct all units under their command, control, or political influence to observe an unconditional cease-fire with effect from the 24th of November; and D, they will facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance. Now, the document as signed has boxes to the right which contain the following passage for your comment, please: "President Slobodan Milosevic committed the SFRY Rump Presidency to directing the JNA to withdraw from Croatia." And, "General Kadijevic committed the JNA's withdrawal from Croatia." And then the next box, second bullet point: "President Milosevic committed paramilitary and irregular forces under his formal and informal authority to observing the cease-fire. Kadijevic committed the JNA to the same regarding paramilitary troops fighting in conjunction with the JNA." Your comment, please, on the role of the Rump Presidency directing the JNA's withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what this is in these boxes. Is that an integral part of the document or is it someone's interpretation of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, the interpreters cannot hear this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, because Mr. Nice is confusing the witness on purpose. The text of the Geneva document does exist. It's legible, and it's clear. And in the boxes are the explanations that they provided here, and they do not coincide with the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop you. Let us discover what the meaning of these various boxes is. Where does that come from, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It comes from the exhibit, as I understand it, but if I'm wrong I will be corrected and perhaps you'd better get the original exhibit that's gone in. They're Okun's comments, as exhibited on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They're Ambassador Okun's comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They are indeed and the Court will remember that he provided a number of comments in this form on documents that he produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this witness should ignore the comments except insofar as he regards them as helpful and he can be asked for his interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is evidence we've heard, you understand, Mr. Jovic, that from -- from Ambassador Okun with whom you're familiar, I think -- that the accused committed the SFRY Rump Presidency to direct the JNA's withdrawal. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I say that Okun can say whatever he wants to say, because Milosevic cannot bind the Rump Presidency in any way. The Rump Presidency sent General Kadijevic on behalf of the organs of the federation and stated that he could sign this kind of document on our behalf, because we wanted the army to withdraw from the barracks in Croatia. Milosevic did not even have to attend the meeting at all. So Kadijevic signed this on behalf of the federation, and that was the position of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the references that Ambassador Okun made on his understanding about paramilitaries under the control or direction of either the accused or Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Paramilitary units from Serbia, if one means by that the volunteer units of Serbia, according to the decision of the Presidency, always had to be under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. There were problems that some were trying to get out of control and not abide by military discipline, but they were duty-bound to be under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army. This here can only be a warning that it should not be permitted for them to remain outside that control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other document at about the same time to be just briefly looked at. It's tab 16 of our Exhibit 596, and it's another UNESCO letter to you thanking you -- lay it on the overhead projector -- for the opportunity to meet and to hear your explanations of events taking place in your country, and explaining that he, the author Daniel Janicot, returned to his director general announcing an intention to send -- and his director general announced an intention to send a permanent UNESCO observer to Dubrovnik. Tab 16, and I'd like now to have your observations, if I can have them, on Dubrovnik, and I'm going to show a couple of videos or short clips of videos to remind the Chamber of evidence that we've seen. Do you accept, Mr. Jovic, that Dubrovnik was shelled by the JNA in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I do not accept it. What I accept is that there were warnings on the part of the world public, especially the Croatian public, that Dubrovnik had been shelled. Of course we were violently opposed to that. We called the military leadership, and we asked for all the circumstances to be investigated. We received detailed information that the army had strict orders that the old part of Dubrovnik cannot be shelled and that they cannot enter it, and that no one indeed did enter the old city or shell it. There were only two shells that came to the old town by accident, but measures were taken against the persons who had fired those shells. However, it's not that anybody ordered that, it's not that the Yugoslav People's Army did that, and the General Staff had never been informed of any such thing. We accepted this information as correct and we believed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show you a few short excerpts from evidence that the Chamber has seen to remind the Chamber and give you an opportunity to comment. The first one is Exhibit 395 or part of it, the ITN report relating to mid-November 1991, produced by Paul Davies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we can now show a small extract from another one, 372, which relates to the 8th of December, and on the evidence we've had, Mr. Jovic, it's filming damage which was its -- filming a film crew that was filming damage on behalf of General Kadijevic. That's what the evidence amounts to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people filming seen on that video were said to have been, on the evidence, filming on behalf of Kadijevic. Now, you were a member of what was the Commander-in-Chief of the army at that time, effectively. Can you help us, please, with whether you were informed about these events or whether you accepted these events occurred even?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: We accepted that two shells strayed into Dubrovnik, and the army established that. What can be seen here is the main street of Dubrovnik. It can be seen that it wasn't damaged at all except for this one building on this street of Stradun. A hole can be seen in front of one particular building, and perhaps a shell fell there. And also there is some rubble. Perhaps that is a consequence of that in one of the smaller streets there. Whether there was more of it and whether there were more shells involved than what Kadijevic had informed us about is something I cannot say on the basis of this film either. I can claim -- I cannot claim that there were more than two shells that the General Staff had told us about or that there were indeed only two shells as they had told us. I have seen this film, but I cannot be certain of anything on the basis of this brief video footage of two minutes. So I'm not in a position to change my attitude towards what the General Staff told us. If the Court has firm evidence that it was otherwise, then they are going to decide accordingly. What I can say is what we had been informed about, and we were staunchly opposed to anyone touching Dubrovnik at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving on to paragraph 104. I may come back to Dubrovnik a little later. In early December of 1991, did you have a conversation with the accused about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, about how easy or difficult the problem would be there?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. We had many discussions. This discussion that is recorded is quite important, because we made an assessment during this discussion that most probably Europe and the international community would soon recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state, that we, since we are constantly being criticised by the international community, although we thought that this criticism was exaggerated, should not allow ourselves to have the Yugoslav People's Army found there because they would be treated as an occupying army, and we don't want that to happen and that we should take measures in order to avoid that. The measures that were assessed to be preventive measures were the following: That citizens of the Yugoslav -- of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia who were born in Serbia and Montenegro should be sent to Serbia and Montenegro, and the other way round. That was the way in which our citizens would not be in the army once Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 105. Did you call up Kadijevic and ask him to join your discussion?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We called him because it was impossible to have this carried out without the military. Mr. Milosevic presented this to him, that it was necessary to redeploy the troops. Kadijevic, whose orientation was a traditional one, that is to say in favour of Yugoslavia and having a mixed ethnic composition in the army throughout the territory, he said that he simply would not accept that and that the General Staff would not accept that. But then it seems that he understood what this was all about. He left, and as The Diary shows, he had this carried out rather quickly with very few exceptions, say 10 or 15 per cent of soldiers from Serbia and Montenegro were still in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the moment when its independence was recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 107. Paramilitaries and your discussion with the accused about Arkan in particular, please. To what extent did the Presidency hear of -- the Rump Presidency hear of paramilitary activity?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we did not treat that as paramilitary units but as volunteer units. According to our regulations, it was allowed that volunteers join the army or that volunteer units be placed under army command at the front line where the war is actually being waged. There was a decision of the Presidency that volunteer units cannot act arbitrarily. They have to be subordinated to the army command. That had to be done within the orders issued by the army. From time to time when the army reported to us about what was going on, they also submitted partial reports, in a few sentences only, about the problems they were encountering with paramilitary units. These were not very long texts, but they boiled down to a few sentences, namely that the paramilitary units were not fully subordinated to the military command and that from time to time they tried to act beyond military discipline. There was never any specific mention of any particular unit, but this phenomenon was referred to in universal terms, as it were. As for my conversation with Mr. Milosevic, I spoke to him once about something that happened very often in public. Arkan, on the one hand, was a dubious person, considered a criminal, and that on the other hand, it was being rumoured that he was in touch with the state organs of Serbia, especially because at that time he started forming paramilitary units or, rather, volunteer units. I asked Mr. Milosevic who this Arkan was and whether he was indeed an extended arm or a close associate of the police of Serbia or other Serb authorities. Mr. Milosevic told me quite directly and without any second thoughts that these were criminals and that we have nothing to do with them. Then I replied to him that this should definitely be cleared up and that we should not lose our good name over that. Later on, it turned out that Arkan had these units of his but that he still maintained some contacts and some connections with the army in the field too, of course, because according to these relations that I already referred to, he had to be in touch with them. The extent to which he had other contacts apart from these within Serbia itself is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, it's not entirely clear to me what you have said about the relationship between the paramilitaries and the army. On one occasion you said the army reported to you that the paramilitaries were not subordinated to them. What do you mean by that? Do you mean that the paramilitaries did not take orders from them or that they were not subject to military discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I spoke about paramilitary units, I always talked about volunteer units from Serbia that went to the front line of their own free will. When I spoke about the army reporting to us that the paramilitary units were not abiding by military discipline and that they had problems with them, I said that in the sense that it was their duty to observe military discipline and to be subordinated to the commander in the field, and that they, the paramilitary units, from time to time tried to evade that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What made it their duty to be so subordinated? What was the basis of that duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of a decision of the Presidency of the SFRY in order to prevent chaos in the field. These individual military units could otherwise operate outside the concept of the defence of the area. They might clash with what the Yugoslav army wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conversation with the accused had him saying that something was going to be done. In the event, was anything ever done by the accused to bring Arkan to heel or to control?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can answer that question because I don't know. But it is true that Arkan set up his volunteer unit just like other people set up their own volunteer units. Now, whether that started independently and a possible cessation of relations with Arkan had they existed or perhaps those relations didn't exist or they were interrupted and re-established perhaps, that would be conjecture and surmise and I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following on from His Honour Judge Robinson's concerns, we can all note that the phrase "state within a state" has been used by you. Can you just explain that.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: As far as Arkan is concerned, Arkan, in the midst of Belgrade, had his guards, and they stood guard around his own house. They wore uniforms, they had weapons. So it was something that wasn't a volunteer unit in the field, it was something that was taking place in the heart of Belgrade. I don't think that was normal, and I think that that was something that irritated the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 108. Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you go on. Mr. Jovic, you also said that Mr. Milosevic said that Arkan was a criminal and that it was unthinkable that official organs would cooperate with someone like Arkan. What did you understand that to mean then? Because on the one hand you have told us that the army felt that the paramilitaries were not subordinated to them. On the other hand, Mr. Milosevic is expressing a view that it was almost unthinkable -- it was unthinkable for official organs to cooperate with someone like Arkan. What in fact was the reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that the volunteer units were not subordinated to the army. What I said was that they tried at times not to adhere to military discipline imposed by the army. And secondly, as far as Arkan himself is concerned, I told you how things stood. I asked Mr. Milosevic, in view of the great criticisms that the public was making with regard to Arkan and the suspicions that he was the extended arm of the police in a way and the fact that people thought he might be a criminal, whether that was true, and whether it was true that Arkan, in one way or another, was linked to the police and was working in cahoots with it. He told me that that was not true, that Arkan was an ordinary criminal, and that he's a common criminal. And I said, well, if they did have some relationships, that they should be stopped so we shouldn't be criticised for things like that. That's what we talked about. Now, what happened next, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, 108 and 109 are not included in the paragraphs we ordered to be given live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this relief. Much thanks, and I'll turn on to page, in the English, 32, paragraph 119.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're moving on again still out of sequence. I'll come back to everything else insofar as I have time later. But we're now up in April of 1992, and I'm wondering if it may not make sense, actually, to -- perhaps if I can just go back and summarise some of the material that's in your statement and, therefore, can be taken as read, starting at paragraph 116 with signing of the Vance Plan, which would be -- was a good thing, you judge, because it would be implemented at a time when all the territory inhabited by the majority Serb population had been liberated. Perhaps you would just help us, please, Mr. Jovic with the term "liberated." You apply "liberated" to the change of control of what type of population and in what setting?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not perhaps the best expression, I must admit, but what I had in mind was the fact that for the most part at that point in time in all parts of Croatia populated by a majority Serb population, the Croatian paramilitary units did not succeed in taking over control. So that would be the essence of what I meant. So still or, rather, again if it hadn't been the case previously, power and authority was in the hands of the local regular organs of the Serbian people, and the Yugoslav People's Army was still located there. So that is the sense of it. Now, the term "liberated" was perhaps not the best choice because I was tired and didn't realise that I had used it, but that is the explanation that I'm giving now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. I think we may find the term elsewhere in your diary and I'm wondering if you could help us with what it reflects as a mind-set, as it's called, or the thinking of the leadership. This is for Serb majority areas where -- in Croatia, where they come under Serb control. How would you describe for us, please, the position of the minority residents in those areas? What happens to them at the time that, although it may be an unhappy word, the Serbs are liberated? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have cleared up the point that the territories were still free territories. Not liberated but free. Now, if a certain territory on which the majority population were the Serbs had been taken control of by Croatian paramilitary units and then was retaken control of by the Serb army or Yugoslav army, only in that case can we say that the territory was liberated once again. So that the explanation is a relative one because you can't liberate yourself, of course, unless somebody has occupied you in the first place. So let's leave it at that, but I do accept that I perhaps used that term erroneously and what I've just explained is the substance of the matter. Now, the question as to what to do with others, never did anybody in the Yugoslav state Presidency and, as far as I know, in the politics and policies pursued by Serbia either, never advocated the position or strove in favour of not having in those territories other people living there too, that other nations should live there too, not only the Serbs, just as it was always our policy to see that in Serbia, which was a multi-nationality or multi-ethnic environment, that all three nationalities should live on a footing of equality. That was never called into question. The only thing was that the territory on which the population was a majority Serb population were still under the power and authority of the Serbs as citizens exercising their power in the local government organs and they did not agree in the decision taken by the Sabor Croatian Assembly by which the Serbs would no longer be a constituent nation, which they had been, and the constitution had been amended contrary to their will, and they did not agree that Croatia secede from Yugoslavia without their will and without solving the Serb question. Otherwise, of course they -- all the other people should remain living where they had lived until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As paragraph 116 makes clear, in your judgement, you were quick to accept the deployment of UN forces because this would have guaranteed the securing of military gains; is that correct, your view?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was. You can interpret things with a certain goal in mind. What was going on there was a war, a civil war, and Serb territories were protected by force from the paramilitary Croatian units. It would have made no sense to wage war constantly and to have to defend oneself from those Croatian paramilitary units all the time. What should have been done was to put a stop to it and seek a political solution. That was the opportune thing to do at that point in time when the Croats were on Croatian territory and the Serbs on Serbian territory. And some sort of political settlement was called for to stop going to war. And what we proposed was to have the UN troops come in until a political settlement be found. So that was the meaning and sense of it, not that they had assumed control of the territory but because it was predominantly a Serb authority on those Serb territories or where the majority population were the Serbs, and that was advantageous to the Serbian people and that they would accept it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Paragraph 117 records acting Secretary of State Eagleburger telling you that the American people will take a long time to forget Vukovar, to which we will return later in your evidence, and also that he couldn't understand why Dubrovnik had been shelled. But over the page in the English version and at the end of this paragraph, you deal with the postulated meeting of the accused and Tudjman at Karadjordjevo. You say you were not present. You declined to discuss it with Eagleburger, and you said at the time that you didn't know what had happened there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you make comment elsewhere in your statement about your views on the accused if in fact there was an agreement at Karadjordjevo where the accused and Tudjman discussed the division of Bosnia if there was such a meeting to such an effect. What's your view on the accused as a result of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a remark to make, Mr. May, an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here in paragraph 117, which Mr. Nice is quoting from, and in fact the witness says quite clearly: "I told him that Serbia was decisively against the break-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it is a pure lie that there were negotiations between Serbia and Croatia on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then he goes on to say: "It is possible that Milosevic and Tudjman did talk at the meeting in Karadjordjevo but as I wasn't there I didn't want to discuss that with Eagleburger." And Nice is now saying that if an agreement was reached, as if the witness said an agreement was reached. He never makes any mention of an agreement, and had there been anything, he must have known about it, whereas he presents the view that we were opposed to the division of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will come back to that after the adjournment. Perhaps, Mr. Nice, you could rephrase it in a way which is as neutral as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. This is the first adjournment during your evidence, and I must warn you, as we warn all witnesses, not to speak to anybody, please, about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand the witness wants to ask you something about contact with his lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can talk about that, of course. Yes. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we begin, during the adjournment, I checked the tab 6 of Prosecution's Exhibit 396. It was an annex of secret council letter, and there were no boxes in there. The comments which is alleged -- asserted as Ambassador Okun's comments, I say that it is an interpretation of the OTP as his comments. So if you -- I don't think we have to put to the witness what other witnesses had stated, but if you'd like to do that, you have to do it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that that error crept in. The document came to me and I understood it to be what it was, but we have the witness's answers, but of course the observations upon which they were founded lose the force of a quotation in the form of a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the question we were asking before the adjournment, we were at, the Chamber will recall, page 32 in the English, paragraph 117. If the Chamber would be good enough to come back, keeping a finger there, to paragraph 71, and if the witness would look at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. May I ask the volume to be put down. It's too loud. That's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although paragraph 71 is one I can take from the witness statement, I was hoping for the witness to give a fresh answer to the proposition so the Chamber could hear it fresh, but the question is here in the text of his statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from paragraph 71, tell the Judges, please, Mr. Jovic, if it were shown that the accused indeed had had a discussion with Tudjman on the partition of Bosnia, would that show that he had withheld that from you; and if so, what would that do to your opinion of the accused?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I should like to say that everything written in that paragraph, and the first thing is this, that I was never informed by Mr. Milosevic that at a possible meeting of that kind they discussed -- he discussed -- possibly discussed with Mr. Tudjman the partition of Bosnia. That's the first point. The second point is that when I heard from Mr. Mesic, when I was given information of this kind which he conveyed to the public, that he was saying what he was saying in order to inflict damage on Tudjman because he had come to a political clash with him. And all the circumstances pointed to the fact that it was highly unlikely that Mr. Milosevic could have discussed anything like that. Now, the third point that I wanted to make is this: Why did I believe Mesic not to be telling the truth? Because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Jovic, because we're very pressed for time and the Judges have heard a lot of other evidence about this, including from Mr. Markovic to whom I want to turn. If the Judges in due course decide that such a meeting occurred and it was kept from you, what does that tell you about the accused? That's the only question, hypothetical, that I want you to deal with.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple: That means that in that case, Milosevic didn't want to inform me about that. But that was highly unlikely, as far as I was concerned, and I should now like to say that that would be another blot in our relationship which otherwise was one of trust and confidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 117 of -- yes, 117. The end of that we have four exhibits, tabs 6, 7, 8, and 9. Have you reviewed from the 21st of February - and we needn't look at any except one of these documents - an invitation for a session of the PSFRY to be held on the 27th of February, exhibit -- tab 7, the minutes in shorthand of the session actually held on the 2nd of March; tab 8, the minutes of the 89th -- 189th session held on that day; and then Exhibit 9, the shorthand notes of the session with representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 2nd of March, item 9. You reviewed all those documents?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have reviewed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they appear to be genuine?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From tab 7, Your Honours, I want to just look at one passage, which I'm going to place on the overhead projector in English, and I'm going to ask the witness to read a passage for us from the original. We can see, if the usher would be good enough, that Mr. Zecevic speaks following Kostic but before Kostic - on the previous page, please - we will see that Mr. Jovic was speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jovic, the document shows that Zecevic spoke just shortly after you did, and can you please now in the original find the passage Zecevic's noted contribution, which begins, "This is a very complex issue." It's further down the page, please. It's on the next page. It must be. Yes. It's the fourth line on the page at the moment and it begins: "This is a very complex issue." Zecevic is speaking, and he says -- do you find this in the original text, please, Mr. Jovic. "This is a very complex issue. Instinctively, everything Croatian was destroyed and burned there in order to prevent them from returning. It is the truth that we cannot live together. We do not want it, and we will not." Now, you were at that meeting in March of 1992, page 78 and 79 of tab 7 in B/C/S, for the accused. Can you explain how something like that could be said in your presence at that meeting, please?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't seem to find that sentence, but from the contents I see that it is there somewhere. It's like this: This is -- these are large stenographic notes numbering some 100 pages, and this can be understood only if one understands the conclusions that were made, and especially if one reads through everything that was stated on the occasion. The substance of the meeting was this: Preparation for the arrival of the UN peacekeepers into the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina and also the tasks and assignments of what should be done when this happens. One of the tasks that we discussed was to ensure all citizens who were persecuted or had to leave their homes for whatever reason to return to their homes and that conditions be provided that they can live and work there normally and that life can continue there normally. And that is stated in the Yugoslav state Presidency conclusions. One of the episodes here was that Mr. Zecevic said, "But we have a village," he said, "in which the Croats live, and they were instinctively expelled." So it wasn't pursuant to a plan or an order, it was that the citizens expelled each other, and in this case it was this group that was expelled. And he was wondering what could be done. He was complaining and wanted to see what could be done. And unfortunately, their property was burnt. And he said that he was afraid that if they come back, it will be very difficult because it was -- inter-nationality relations were such that they would have found it difficult to co-exist together. So the conclusions we made was that everybody was to return to where they had originally lived and that conditions should be provided for them to live and work normally. And if anything -- any property was burnt, it would have to be rebuilt again. That was the conclusion that the Presidency made. And the man said what he said. The conclusion was along the lines of the sole political option possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so that I can understand it and then we'll move on, that's your explanation of the phrase "Destroyed and burned there in order to prevent them from returning"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Instinctively. And I insist upon the word. He said instinctively, not that it was planned by the authorities or ordered by anyone, but instinctively, which means the revolt of the Serb people towards them because they had come to loggerheads between themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which page is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 79 in that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the English version, I think it is page 84 of 149. No. Ms. Dicklich tells me I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can find the number ending with ET number 2829.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I move on to four exhibits that Your Honours will want to know are late provided, although they have been viewed with the witness, because they were, until I think yesterday, under the grip of Rule 70. They're tabs 10, 11, 12, and 13. I can summarise them because the witness has reviewed them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On most of the pages that I was provided in English, there is no ERN number or any other number or the page number either. So probably this was done in haste and omitted in haste. But it is very difficult to find my way around if you don't read through the whole text. I can show you the pages, and where I show you this document there's Gligorovic, Kostic, Grigorijevic, Kostic, and so on, but nowhere do I see a single reference, and you can take a look at my copy in the English version to the page number, or ERN number, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's unpaginated. It's unpaginated. Perhaps you could have a look at that over the adjournment so we can make sure we can follow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to tabs 10 to -- 10, 11, 12, and 13, is it right, Mr. Jovic, that you've reviewed a letter Mendiluce UNHCR dated the 19th of March, 1992, drawing to your attention a number of recent incidents? To that, did you reply -- no. Is there another letter that you've reviewed of yours dated April the 28th of 1992 to General Nambiar referring to a letter of his from April the 24th in which he draws to your attention cases of violent expulsion of citizens of Croatian nationality from their homes and refers to a letter of Mr. Thornberry, and you express your resolve to prevent all forms of forcible eviction. You then reviewed another letter from Mr. Thornberry of the 25th of June of 1992, where he deals with 232 people of Croatian origin, including 160 wounded taken prisoner during Vukovar and for whom news was sought. And have you then reviewed a letter not by you but by Mile Pesut to Mr. Thornberry dealing with those concerns?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen those letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so by those letters and your replies which can be studied in full if appropriate, you were put on notice about international concern about forcible eviction and, in particular, about people missing from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: We reacted to every letter we received, and what we did was we took steps with the relevant organs for them to look into the matter and to prepare responses to the UN organs and measures to be taken to prevent what was going on and what our attention was being drawn to in the letters. And we informed Mr. Thornberry and Mr. Nambiar immediately about that and those letters speak about that and speak about those matters at greater length, because they mention several hundred people, without saying who they were, just the numbers from Vukovar, and in our reply we said that all the people that came into the hands of our army, we told them where they were, where those people were transported to, how many of them were cared for, received treatment, how many exchanged, and so on. So detailed information and reports were sent out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just help me with this, please, Mr. Jovic, before we move on. You know the nature of the allegations about Vukovar generally. Do you accept now that this massacre occurred, and if it did, of course it occurred at a time when you were part of the Commander-in-Chief of the army. Do you accept that it occurred?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I was never informed about that while I occupied my post. Much later, I learnt about this from the information media or, rather, from the work of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you offer any explanation, just to help us, with how, if the JNA were involved and you were the Commander-in-Chief, that this never came to your attention at all? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this conditional "if the army were involved," that is a hypothetical, and to the best of our knowledge, what we -- according to what we did, the army did not have orders to do anything like that. On the contrary, it had a strict ban on doing anything like that. And we don't know that anybody from the army ordered that or that anybody from the army carried it out. That's what I can say, and it is up to the Court to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or your successors, to your knowledge, order an inquiry into the circumstances of the Vukovar massacre that led to a report?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: We were not informed about that, about any massacre, so we could not have given any orders under those circumstances. What happened subsequently, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 119, which has to be given in full, and 120, I think. 30th of April, 1992, was there a conversation involving Kostic, the accused, Bulatovic, Zivota Panic who now replaced Adzic, and including Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, such a meeting was held, such a conversation did take place. It took place, and basically this was a discussion during which agreement was supposed to be reached as to what should be done with the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the situation when the international community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state. We already said that we in Serbia, Mr. Milosevic and I, thought that we should not allow by any means for there to be a procrastination in this respect, because we would have been attacked for that, and we were under attack anyway with reason and without reason, so we held this meeting in order to see how we would withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina all citizens of Serbia and Montenegro. Let me clarify this. The army of Yugoslavia consists of the citizens of all republics. As Yugoslavia fell apart, in terms of facilities, equipment, and personnel, they belonged to the appropriate republics. So the -- so Serbia and Montenegro were only entitled to their own citizens, to the facilities and equipment that were located in Serbia. Of course in that situation, our only obligation was vis-a-vis all the citizens of Serb and Montenegrin ethnicity, to get them out of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to return them home. This decision was passed, and the deadline involved was 15 days. As for the people in Bosnia, they were supposed to decide about their own citizens, their own facilities, their own equipment, their own army, because that is what the international community decided, that they were, an independent state. Of course --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was the question of the wages and pensions and so on for the military raised; and if so, with what resolution?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the expenses of the military until then were financed from the federal budget. So the army did belong to the federal budget, and all the officers and soldiers were paid out of that budget and everything else was paid out of the federal budget because the army was a common army. Of course, then people from Bosnia raised the question of how they would act then. We realised that there was a problem, but we did not discuss it then. We only discussed the return of Serbs and Montenegrins to their homes from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Mladic moved as a result of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the following way: It was established that General Vukovic, who was the military commander in the area, was a Serb and therefore he had to be withdrawn. Then they said, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, that they would then appoint Mr. Mladic as commander. And we consider that to be their decision and we did not make any comments to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what frequency did the accused have contact with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is what he and Karadzic would have to be asked, because I haven't got any records of this nature. I can assume, though, that their contacts had to exist in relation to humanitarian aid that Bosnia had constantly expected from Serbia because it was a country in war and under a blockade. And also, there were peace initiatives, and the international community always asked for Milosevic to take part in this. It was also natural for him to take part in this because Serbia was under sanctions before the war in Bosnia was brought to an end. And those are probably the reasons that made it necessary for them to be in contact often. That is a general answer, but I really do not know with what exact frequency they met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 124 and following. On the nature of the accused, substantially drawn from your second book, the Book on Milosevic. The Court will see here many pages to get through. I'm going to ask the witness to deal with these issues very briefly. Paragraph 124, the accused as a democrat or an autocrat, please; your comments.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: These are very unpleasant questions for me here before this Court. In the book, I struck a balance in terms of his own traits, if that is what this is about -- this is a personal opinion of mine and they cannot and should not serve as a basis for anybody's judgement. The entire book as a whole can be used by someone to see what my opinion of Milosevic is, except for the facts that I refer to in the book as well. As for my assessment of Mr. Milosevic, he was an undisputed leader. He was recognised by the citizens, by the population, and he was elected with a vast majority in the elections. He was very intelligent, a very capable statesman, but in my opinion, he was inclined towards reaching even major decisions without consulting even the organs that are in charge of that. So many decision were passed on the basis of his authority and some were wrong. That is what my assessment would be. Of course, my assessment is my assessment, but it is up to others to accept this or not accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you regard yourself as a close if not his closest associate for many years; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still on paragraph 124. To what degree was the accused able to dispose of people once he'd finished using them for a particular purpose?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Regrettably, this is what was done often in the leaderships of our party and our governments and our Assemblies. A great many people went through them, and they are no longer present in politics, not in traces, and quite a few people who were involved in politics were dismissed by him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what degree did retention of power personally drive him?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question. Could you please clarify it a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what degree was his retaining power, his remaining in power, a goal of his?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is the objective of any politician to retain power. But if this is viewed in the context of achieving programme objectives or perhaps sacrificing some programme objectives in order to retain power, I think that in that case, advantage would be given to retaining power rather than abiding by programme objectives and goals. I think that that assessment would be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
