utterances.text: Paragraph 125, last sentence. To what extent did he find himself surrounded by people who would not only obey but also perhaps glorify him?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is a natural consequence. If a person that has a very strong personality is convinced that he can reach decisions on his own, conceive of them on his own and defend them - if we were to go into great detail, perhaps it would be a bit labourious - then it would only be natural for such a person to focus on persons who would simply be carrying out his decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Those who would not change the decisions in any way. That is the kind of selection that would be made, people who would be willing to carry out these decisions and, finally, to be part of a team that is working towards the attainment of those objectives. Therefore, in my opinion, this selection was based on taking trustworthy people who would carry out the decisions made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a personality cult at some stage with, I think, people carrying photographs of you. How did the personality cult develop for the accused?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was sometime in 1988 and 1989 when there were big rallies held in Serbia demanding the persecutions of Serbs to be stopped in Kosovo, and perhaps this was the biggest exodus that ever took place in Europe, the Serbs leaving Kosovo, but Europe was unwilling to see it or unwilling to say or do anything about it. Milosevic was practically the first one to start dealing with that problem and to try to stop this. And he enjoyed the massive support of citizens. At these rallies they carried photographs, big photographs of Milosevic and of a few other prominent officials. On one occasion, I asked Milosevic for have this -- to have this brought to an end, because we had had enough of a personality cult with Stalin, with Tito, and we were not supposed to repeat this choreography, so -- Milosevic did not really say anything about it. I saw that something was done about it, though. All the other pictures were removed, and his stayed on. And the personality cult in -- was, therefore, even enhanced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 128. Communist, socialist, and to what degree did he care about the principles of social justice?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: We had a programme of the Socialist Party, and Mr. Milosevic was the president of the party. The main objective of this programme was the idea of social justice. Regrettably, in the period that we are talking about, those ten years or so, especially over the last five or six years, there were grave sanctions that were imposed on the country, and all of the people became impoverished, but a very narrow circle got very rich. So the divide between the very few very rich people and the vast majority of the poor people grew further. And I characterise this as a failure in terms of the programme that we had established. And in some way, the party that was in power had to be held responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 129. To what degree was he a nationalist; and then at the end of that paragraph, if you can deal with this issue for the learned Judges, how did he deal with state controlled businesses and why?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: As regards nationalism, Mr. Milosevic quite certainly, and I'm saying this not by way of a personal assessment, but I am really convinced of this, that he always advocated and pursued in practice the position that nobody should be handicapped or persecuted because he's a Serb. Everybody had to be equal. He was not a chauvinist, never. You can be sure of that. He was decidedly against separatism. Not because somebody is of a different ethnic background but because they wanted to secede. I'm talking about Serbia proper now. The secession of Slovenia, Croatia, et cetera, is a completely different matter. So he was not a nationalist, he was not a chauvinist. He never agreed with anything being done against someone because he's not a Serb or that he should not be equal because of that, that's for sure. As for his attitude towards socially owned property, our factories, for the most part, practically all of them, were socially owned property, as it was called. In a way, it was state owned but the form was slightly different, and the state had a dominant influence in terms of appointing directors, managers, and regulating the conditions for economic performance. However, by virtue of the fact that the state was influential in terms of personnel decisions, it could also use its influence in terms of the allocations made in the area. So this was the material base of power. The Socialist Party of Serbia did not have its own companies, it did not have its own property or its own capital from which it would be financed. And it is only natural that members of the Socialist Party who were in high positions in these factories were an important factor in terms of its importance. They could decide who they would assist, et cetera. But this economy was getting weaker and weaker by the day, due to sanctions but also due to the very concept underlying the economy. It did not have the strength to move on as a private economy would. I think I cannot make any claims to this effect, but I think that Mr. Milosevic felt this. On the other hand, there were new privately owned enterprises held by the so-called nouveau riche. And again, this is my very own opinion: Mr. Milosevic I think believed that it would be very dangerous for our policies if this new economy were to get a political representative of their own, their own political parties that could suppress us with the material strength that they would have, because one always needed resources. He pursued a policy of having these owners get closer to him and thereby be under his control as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 132, control of mass media, television, radio, newspapers. You refer earlier in your statement to writing articles about Markovic, I think it is. Tell us about the accused's influence over or control over media.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Please, let it be clear: The most important media in our country, in Serbia - because I'm talking about Serbia - those that have a crucial impact on citizens were TV Belgrade, Radio Belgrade, and up to a degree, the Politika daily, which is the major newspaper in the country. It is true that we had hundreds of other media that were not under government control and under Milosevic's influence. They were opposition media. But they were not that far-reaching as far as radio and television was concerned. Their broadcasts were not that extensive, and the circulation of these newspapers was negligible. So the most important reason was that TV Serbia reached every home, whereas local stations only reached very limited local areas. As for the influence of Mr. Milosevic over state television and state radio and the Politika daily, it was a major influence, a decisive influence. That is true, and that is what was predominant in terms of how people were informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he use the media to elevate or undermine his fellow Serb leaders - just yes or no - and if so, have you in your book given examples of how he did that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent to which this was necessary in terms of pursuing policy, the media were used, of course. There were situations, there were times when Mr. Milan Babic was so obstinate that did he not want to accept the Vance Plan, and of course the media had to be involved in persuading the people that Babic had to be replaced because this was against the interest of the Serb people. Then there would come another time when somebody else was supposed to be chosen, and it was assessed that Mr. Martic could be the person, and then of course the media perhaps promoted Martic to a greater extent perhaps than he had actually deserved by way of his activity until then. And so on and so forth. This was referred to in the book and explained in the book. Of course the media were always used in the interest of the policy that was being pursued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, we are concerned here, Mr. Jovic, and we discussed this the last few days, with, if the Prosecution case is right, the most terrible crimes being committed by people over a short period of time, and it may or may not be that there will be evidence about how that mechanism operates. Just for this purpose, was the accused aware of the power of media on the people he led?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course he was aware of it. Mr. Milosevic, by virtue of the fact that he attempted and succeeded in influencing to a great degree the orientation of the media that I refer to, TV, radio, and the Politika daily, he did understand what the mood of the people was. I don't know in which context grave crimes are exactly being referred to now, but this is information and political activity directed at the citizens, at the general public. We're talking about media in Serbia. We -- this did not go beyond Serbia except marginally, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to the phrase "What is not published does not happen at all." Can you amplify that for us, please? Paragraph 134.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: That is a - how should I put this? - a slogan, a phrase that Mr. Milosevic espoused. He thought that if citizens were informed about something, then they knew that it happened, and if they were not informed, then simply they did not deal with such issues, and he simply thought that it was very important for state television and radio to report primarily in the interest of current politics. So if something is not in the interest of current politics, it doesn't have to be published.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs 135, 136 and following, to what degree did the accused regard the party, the SPS, as his property? To what degree did party activity cease to be, at some stage, real activity, or real democratic activity?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this has to do with what I spoke of earlier, the method that Mr. Milosevic applied basically in decision-making. Of course, according to the statute of the Socialist Party, it was envisaged that decisions, main decisions, should be reached by the Congress and then by the Main Committee between two Congresses. Then there is also an Executive Committee that is in charge of carrying these decisions out in practice. The problem was that in a way from the 3rd Congress onwards, and especially at the 3rd Congress, in my opinion, the democratic way of choosing people into the leadership was abandoned. Lists of candidates for the Main Committee were under strict control according to the characteristics of people who would be eligible. Others simply could not be elected. And then after that, it would be very easy at the meeting of the Main Committee, and that is the committee that operated between two Congresses, that any meeting of the Main Committee, any decision that was proposed would be accepted even without a debate, or if there were a debate, there weren't any dissenting voices. This happened because, in my opinion, candidates for the Main Committee were only people who would act in that way, who would not create any problems in terms of what was being proposed originally. However, unfortunately, a single person cannot be infallible under such circumstances, no matter how intelligent and how capable, as was the case of Mr. Milosevic, and it was proven that there were many mistakes that were made in this policy. It is for such mistakes that people lose power, and ultimately he did lose power. Of course this doesn't have anything to do with other matters, but it does have to do with confidence and the loss of power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 136 is your language. Can you review it and tell us if you adopt it.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I was talking about. I do agree. That is the essence of the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Party activity turned into a farce" is the phrase. Then if we can move on. I think you by implication already dealt with the power of the Presidency of the SPS. You held that position for a time when the accused wasn't able to hold it for constitutional reasons. The rest of the time he held it, or part of the rest of the time. And you contrast the power that he had when president of the party with the power you had. In a sentence or so, could you just explain that?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: Mr. Milosevic was the absolute authority regardless of whether he was party president or not. Not a single important decision in Serbia was taken without him nor could it have been made without him, either when I was president or when I wasn't president. Therefore, we always respected his opinions as the number one man, regardless of the fact that he wasn't president of the party at that time. And he personally was very interested in everything, and he didn't agree that decisions be made without his taking part. And of course, that problem never arose. We didn't put things that way at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 139. You say -- you deal with his monopoly on personal politics in all institutions. Is there anything you want to add about that, please?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: That was the way he functioned and ruled, and in view of the fact that the method of ruling, or power and authority was, in fact, a way not of selecting people who would debate subject matter from different aspects and bring in the best decisions but people who would be obedient. And if you have a situation of that kind, then you need people you can trust. So he had to have people who he could trust to accept the decisions he made. So cadres policy for this method of work was necessary, and Mr. Milosevic understood that very well. And he paid strict attention to who was on the list for the main party board and who the candidates were for the popular deputies and the list of candidates for the government of the Republic of Serbia and the list of candidates for federal deputy, and so on and so forth, all positions where decisions were made. He took care of all that because he didn't want to clash with anybody with respect to the policies he wished to wage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 143. His control over Montenegrin leaders, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the leaders from Montenegro were relatively independent in Montenegro. They were autonomous, but they had a proper form of cooperation with Serbia over the long run, and with Mr. Milosevic himself. That was looking at it in general terms. That would be generally correct. Because they had come to power on the wave of changes that took place in Serbia at the end of the 1980s, for instance, and Mr. Milosevic headed those changes. So in a way, they were in Montenegro what we ourselves were in Serbia, and from that, the nature of the cooperation emerged and was based on those grounds. Of course, they were from similar kindred parties, that is to say the League of Communists of Serbia and the League of Communists of Montenegro, and that was quite understandable. Now, somewhat later on some conflicts did arise, and I mention the fact that there was not complete agreement on all matters. For example, when the federal constitution of Yugoslavia was being drawn up, the leaders of Montenegro aspired towards great autonomy for the republics. They wanted to see the republics have at least as much power and independence as they had in the SFRY, whereas Mr. Milosevic and I myself, I agreed with him there, we worked together, we thought that we ought to strengthen the federation because the federation up until that time, the SFRY, had some serious weaknesses in its power and competence. So it wasn't able to function properly at all times. A compromise was found, but what I want to say is that there was not an identity of opinions on all matters. And a similar situation arose when I mentioned the Carrington Plan, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 144. You deal with the ability of republican bodies, of federal bodies -- of the employees of federal bodies to be dismissed. Can you just deal with that, please. Perhaps I should say the vulnerability of the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection to make, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not believe that the witness could have said that they had -- I had the power and authority to dismiss functionaries in federal organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let the witness give his evidence. Yes. What was the question you wanted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know from the witness the circumstances in which federal employees could be dismissed if they didn't act on the decisions of their respective republics.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably it wasn't federal employees. It was functionaries from the republics in the federation. So if that's what that is about, then I shall be happy to explain. The members of the Yugoslav state Presidency were elected by the Assembly of Serbia, so it is the Assembly of Serbia electing that body and dismissing it. The Federal Assembly just takes note of those elections and they become members of the SFRY. That's the first point. The second point is that the members of the Yugoslav state Presidency are duty-bound to coordinate relations within the federation by means of the fact that the positions taken by their republics would be advocated in the federation and a compromise solution sought which would be in the interests of one and all. In that way, the members of the Yugoslav state Presidency can only function successfully if what they advocate there is advocated and promoted by their own republic. Otherwise, to the contrary, we'd have an impossible situation in which the Yugoslav state Presidency makes a decision on a matter, whereas the republic that one of the Presidency members represents says, "That's not our view. That's not what we want and what we advocate." So that is not possible on a legal basis. So under those conditions, each republic has the right to dismiss the Presidency representative if he deviates from the interests of that particular republic. And this is precisely what happened when Croatia replaced Stipe Suvar, for example, who was an elected Yugoslav state Presidency member, and he was in office for approximately a year, and then sent Stipe Mesic to replace him, who was better able and they considered that he would be better capable of representing their interests. So representing the interests of a republic is a constitutional duty, and the republic does have the right to replace its own representative. Now, who it's going to put forward is another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just dealing with Mr. Mesic, he says how it was that you would refer, apparently in the course of meetings, back to Belgrade and to the accused, and I think you accept in your statement you would have done so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In meetings we've heard how you would leave meetings in order to be able to make phone calls and then come back.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you accept that you did that because you had to refer to the accused for instructions or advice?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never said that, and that's not true. I was in constant communication with Mr. Milosevic in building up our policies and positions. I would never leave Presidency meetings to go and telephone to Mr. Milosevic to ask him whether I was allowed to act in one way or another. That's just insinuation on somebody's part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 145, please. You deal with the promotion of the obedient by the accused. You may have touched already on this, but you used the phrase "political purges" in your book, so perhaps you'd just help us with that.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I explained that in my book. There were several cases to the effect that people were dismissed, replaced if they were no longer needed or what they said or the things they did did not suit or they had accomplished what they were expected to do and were no longer elected. And there were cases of direct replacement without any explanations given. But mostly a method was applied by which people were used while they had a use and while they were willing not to make any complications, and they were done away with when that was no longer the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the national parliament, paragraph 146, how did the accused deal with those who thought differently from the thinking of his government?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about the Federal Assembly, we're talking about the republican Assembly. Mr. Milosevic couldn't do anything along those lines in the Federal Assembly. Of course, he could withdraw his own deputies but he couldn't change the composition of the entire Assembly. What we're talking about here is his right as president of the republic to disband the Assembly, the parliament, which he used at the time. And what happened was that there was an organised, heated debate in the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia about the work of the government, and there was endless criticism which went on for several days or weeks. And Mr. Milosevic decided to disband the Assembly or parliament and to elect a new one, and this state of affairs was cut short with that act. That's one fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with some of the things comparatively briefly: The history of the appointment or selection of Milan Panic and his removal from office, he being somebody from America, otherwise unknown in former Yugoslavia. Is that an example of the accused's control of individuals? It's dealt with between paragraphs 147 and 149.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a drastic example, if you will. Mr. Milosevic enjoyed great authority within the party and he wielded that authority and the decisions were taken which were not sometimes checked out fully. One of those decisions was the proposal for us to elect Milan Panic as Prime Minister of the federal government. The procedure was such that our Executive Board in the party should okay that, and then our deputy group, which enjoyed the majority in parliament, together I think with another party, should have accepted that. There were quite a lot of difficulties at the Executive Board to have this explained to the members, because nobody knew who the man was. And I found myself explaining something I didn't know about. I told them what Milosevic had told me. And this went through. In the deputy's club it was very difficult to pull that through, and we did vote on it, but there was a great deal of criticism, and the whole thing went through respecting and in fact using Mr. Milosevic's authority or that authority being wielded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to try to get through the end of this section -- I don't know how -- to what hour we're going to be able to sit today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think there may be another hearing in, so as quickly as you can, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm going to trespass into tomorrow but I hope not by much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is simply a limit to the degree to which I can require the witness to go too fast over this material if it has to be given in the ordinary way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can you just help us with a tiny detail at the end of paragraph 150. You explained about your being dismissed and therefore barred festivities and so on. Something happened actually to a tape. Your image was removed from a tape. Can you just explain that and what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as to festivities and tapes, those are all marginal issues. The fact of the matter is that I was replaced, like many others, without any explanation given and without any voting taken and without the right to appeal and without a written decision. Therefore, in a non-democratic way in the party. And I was forced to tender my resignation to the post of popular deputy. Of course the repercussions went further because I was isolated in all kinds of ways from society, and that is one detail. For example, I was never invited to attend state festivities although I was president of the Assembly of Serbia and of Yugoslavia and I held a series of other positions. And if you will, it went so far that when an official holiday was proclaimed, the day we amended the constitution, and I was president of the Assembly and constitutional committee and proclaimed the amendments to the constitution, and I myself was not invited to that national holiday let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your image was erased from some tapes you're saying here. I just want you to explain that.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a tape on the proclamation of the constitution. That is to say the date when a national holiday was proclaimed. And each year when footage was shown of that session, it was shown without my image, without me being there, although I delivered the speech and I was up at the rostrum. So what the footage showed was all the people applauding but not the person actually delivering the speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally on this point, although you have been very robust about being excluded from national events, so that the Judges, who may have no experience of this type of state can understand things, was there an incident involving a local school that was being opened where you were -- where your presence was restricted?

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: First let's clarify one thing: I never protested for not having been invited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I said -- you were being robust.

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said you were being robust about it, you put up with it. Just tell us about --

utterances.speaker: BORISAV JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did accept it as a fact that I didn't have any influence on. I didn't feel happy about it, but I didn't protest at all. And as far as the local school is concerned, I mentioned that during the discussion, during our conversation as one example. At that time, what was being celebrated was the end of construction on a primary school in my local village, town, and the people in charge of the organisation came in from town and from the republic and from the municipality to attend the celebration, and they came and told me that I shouldn't be angry, but they just couldn't invite me to attend the celebration because they were told, "If you invite Boro Jovic to attend the celebration, there will be no celebration." So this was a method they used, a sort retaliation. I don't consider it to be a crime of any kind, just a method of work which was not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It just paints the picture for us, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber is looking for a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we must come to it now, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will finish this passage in, I think, a short period of time tomorrow. I will review the extent, if any, to which I will seek to go over earlier ground but there are one or two topics and just one or two exhibits I haven't covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn until tomorrow. Mr. Jovic, could you be back, please, at 9.00 tomorrow morning to continue your evidence.
